name: 2D map: base map, side panel and map controls
plain: The 2D map shows Puerto Rico on an OpenStreetMap base map. A side panel has eight tabs: Overview, Layers, Catalog, Municipality, Rankings, Transit, Economy and About. A top bar links to the 3D view, the Housing page and the data dictionary.
definition: The base map is OpenFreeMap vector tiles in the OpenMapTiles schema, made from OpenStreetMap data and drawn by MapLibre GL JS under every other layer. It opens on the 'Positron' style, a light map for data; the 'Base map' choice, first in the Territory group of the Map layers tab, switches to another OpenFreeMap style ('Liberty', detailed, with streets, places and buildings; 'Bright', colorful; 'Dark'; 'Fiord', dark blue), to a map of the USGS National Map (aerial imagery, topographic or shaded relief: picture tiles of its own, with no OpenStreetMap data, which the map inspector cannot read) or to no base map (the data alone, on a plain background, with 'Base map off' in the credit line). The choice changes only the base map, is kept in the page address (bm=positron, liberty, bright, dark, fiord, imagery, topo, relief or none) and in the link to the 3D view, and is remembered in this browser as the default for the next visit. It is added once the map is ready, so the data come first; a short 'Loading the base map…' note shows in the credit line until it appears. The map opens on all of Puerto Rico. Zoom buttons and a scale bar with a metric and an imperial scale sit at the bottom right, with the credit lines of the base map ('© OpenStreetMap contributors · © OpenMapTiles · OpenFreeMap', or on a USGS map 'Base map: U.S. Geological Survey, National Geospatial Program') and of the layers that are switched on. The top bar holds the search box, the 'Ask' chat button, links to the 3D + Time view, the Housing page and the data dictionary, and a label such as 'Snapshot 2026-10' that names the build of the data files the page shows. Hover over the label to see the build date. Transit timetables, routes and stops are refreshed every night and are not tied to that label. The codes below list the other details of the page.

coverage.frequency: Base map tiles are requested from OpenFreeMap while you browse. The data layers are rebuilt with each snapshot.

method: app.js builds the map with Leaflet 1.9.4, up to zoom 19. Once the map is ready it loads site/js/core/basemap.js, the one configuration of every base map, which loads MapLibre GL JS 4.7.1 (the same file as the 3D view) and MapLibre GL Leaflet 0.1.4 and draws the OpenFreeMap style in Leaflet's tile pane, under every overlay pane. The base map does not answer clicks: every click goes to the observatory's layers, as before. If the browser has no WebGL, the style does not load within 30 seconds or eight tile requests in a row fail, the base map is removed, the map keeps its layers over a plain light background and a message says 'Base map unavailable'; the map never falls back to the OpenStreetMap Foundation's own tile servers. The opening view fits the box from 17.86 N, 67.30 W to 18.52 N, 65.20 W. Each overlay has its own stacking level, so flood zones and routes draw above land use and protected areas. common.js runs the panel, the tabs (following the accessible tab pattern of the Web Accessibility Initiative, WAI-ARIA) and the help boxes. docs/basemap.md describes the base map.
how_to_read: Use the credit lines in the attribution box when you share a picture of the map. Every dictionary entry has a Cite button. On an entry for a layer or tool it cites that control and names its sources. To cite the data themselves, use the Cite button on the dataset entries listed under Related.
caveats: The base map is made from OpenStreetMap, mapped by volunteers. It shows roads and place names, not official boundaries.

The page needs JavaScript and an internet connection. The map code, the fonts and the base map tiles come from other servers. If the map code does not load, the page says so and offers 'try again'. If the base map cannot be drawn (no WebGL, or OpenFreeMap does not answer), the data still show, over a plain background.
The snapshot label covers the files built together. It does not say when each source last changed.

values.Panel and keyboard: The panel's tabs change with a click or with the left and right arrow keys. Press / to jump to the search box.
values.Phone: On a phone the panel stays hidden until you press the menu button. It closes with its close button, a tap on the grey backdrop or the Escape key.
values.Top bar links: Map (this page), 3D + Time, Housing and Data dictionary. The Data dictionary link opens dictionary.html, the page for definitions, sources, licenses and citations.
values.Files and loading: The page opens with only the municipal boundaries. Its first load is the build information, the municipality statistics, the boundaries and the catalog (about 0.16 MB compressed in Snapshot 2026-10). Every layer, the tourism places included, loads its data file the first time you switch it on (1 MB is 1 million bytes). In Snapshot 2026-10 the largest are land use (about 17.7 MB), the tourism place listings (about 16.7 MB, plus a 0.3 MB file of transit access), flood zones (about 8.0 MB) and protected areas (about 1.5 MB). If a file cannot be loaded, the layer's switch turns itself off and a message appears.
values.Inside another page: When the map sits inside another web page, the mouse wheel scrolls that page until you click the map.

source_detail: Credit lines are drawn by each layer, so they depend on which layers are on. Base map credit line: '© OpenStreetMap contributors · © OpenMapTiles · OpenFreeMap'; on a USGS map, 'Base map: U.S. Geological Survey, National Geospatial Program', with 'Orthoimagery: USDA, USGS' on the aerial imagery. Page code: app.js, network.js, economy.js, chat.js and common.js. The entry of each layer names its data file.

name: About tab and top bar (2D map and 3D view)
plain: The About tab explains what the PR Data Observatory is, who it is for, how to start and how to cite it. It says that Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) developed the observatory as a tool for public use and benefit. It also shows seven headline counts.
definition: The 2D map's About tab has these parts, in order. An introduction says what the observatory is and that it is free, needs no account and is built from open and public data. Seven counts follow. Then come a list of the fields the observatory covers (written from the registry, so it grows with the observatory); a list of four groups the observatory is for; six 'Start here' steps, with buttons for the chat and the data dictionary; five example questions for the chat; a guide to the eight tabs and to the top bar; a note on where the data come from; six 'Keep in mind' points; and a privacy note. The tab ends with a closing section that gives the citation line and the current snapshot, and says where to send a correction or a dataset to add. Five of the seven counts come from meta.json when the page loads. The other two come from dictionary_summary.json when the tab is first opened. The 3D + Time view has its own About tab. It has a short description, a 'How to use it' list of five items (move around, pick a clock, turn layers on and off, plan a route, see it in 2D) and a 'Sources, licenses and how to cite' section with a button that opens the data dictionary. The codes below list the counts and summarise each part.

coverage.frequency: The five counts from meta.json are rebuilt with each snapshot. The two dictionary counts change when the dictionary changes.

method: app.js (renderAbout, loadAboutNumbers). The five counts are read from data/meta.json. The two dictionary counts are fetched from data/dictionary_summary.json the first time the tab is opened, and they are left out if the file does not load. The texts are in index.html and 3d.html. The tab's cite line reads 'Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory' followed by the snapshot label. The last line of the tab gives the same label and the build date.
source_detail: meta.json (counts, network and transport fields) and dictionary_summary.json (the number of dictionary items and of data sources). Cite line on the tab: 'Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, <snapshot label>'. The tab asks you to credit the original sources as well, which the data dictionary writes out.
how_to_read: Quote a count with the snapshot label. The tourism place count follows the default counting rules (see Related), not the filters you set on the Map layers tab.
caveats: The counts are the observatory's own counts of listings and mapped points. They are not counts of businesses, visitors or services in operation.
The stops-and-stations count includes stops of operators whose timetable has expired and stops that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap.

The tab calls the observatory free, with no account, and built from open and public data. It also says that not every source has an open license: some, such as the municipal transit feeds and the Junta de Planificación's maps, state no license.
The tab also says that hazards are mapped zones, that timetables are not live and that survey numbers are estimates. The entries on those layers give the details.

The tab suggests setting disaster and federal money beside housing and the economy. Federal and recovery amounts in the observatory are amounts obligated (committed) or approved. They are not money spent, damage or need.

The Privacy section says that what you type in the search box or the chat stays in your browser, except the online address lookup. The chat also has a button that opens a GitHub request form with your unanswered questions in the web address. See the entry on what the chat keeps on your device.

values.Data sources, each with its license: The number of data sources in the dictionary, not counting software and base-map sources. It is read from dictionary_summary.json.
values.What the observatory covers: A list of the fields (domains) of the registry with their descriptions, written when the page loads, so a new field appears with no change to the page. A field with no data yet is marked. A line under the list says that the observatory keeps growing.
values.Who the observatory is for: The tab names four groups: residents and community groups; local and island planners; researchers, students and journalists; and funders, nonprofits and recovery teams.
values.Start here: six steps: 1. Start with the overview (the Topics tab gives one headline figure for each field; the Catalog tab finds any dataset and adds it to the map). 2. Turn on layers (Map layers tab). 3. Click a municipality or a place (Municipality tab). 4. Put economic data on the map (Analysis tab). 5. Ask a question (the Ask button, in English or Spanish). 6. Check and share: open the Data dictionary, copy a link and download tables as comma-separated values (CSV) files.
values.Questions to try: Where is unemployment highest? Show poverty and unemployment together. Tell me about Ponce. What are the most interesting patterns? What data is missing?
values.The eight tabs, as the About tab describ: Overview (one headline figure for each field, with a trend), Layers (map layers, and shading by any of the measures in the menu), Catalog (search everything the observatory documents, filter it and add it to the map), Municipality (the profile of one municipality), Rankings (rank the 78 municipalities and download the table), Transit (operators and the state of their timetables, vehicles on schedule, residents far from service and a route planner), Economy (the tab says 'more than 100 yearly datasets'; there are 103 in Snapshot 2026-10) and About.
values.The top bar, as the About tab describes: Search (press / to jump to it); Ask (a chat that builds every answer from the data loaded on the page and is not generative artificial intelligence); Map; 3D + Time; Housing; and Data dictionary (what every dataset, variable and measure means, its source and license, the glossary, the published data files and how to cite).
values.Keep in mind: Six points: it is a snapshot; places are listings, not a census of businesses; hazards are mapped zones; timetables are not live; survey numbers are estimates; and patterns are not causes. The last point adds that the observatory is for asking better questions and planning, not a legal, financial or engineering determination.
values.Privacy: No accounts. What you type in the search box or the chat stays in your browser, except the online address lookup, which sends that text to OpenStreetMap's Nominatim service. Like any web page, the observatory loads fonts, code libraries and map tiles from other servers (the tab names Google Fonts, cdnjs, OpenStreetMap and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, NOAA), which can see your Internet Protocol (IP) address.
values.Cite it and tell us what is missing: To cite: Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, followed by the snapshot label. The tab asks you to credit the original sources too, and says the data dictionary writes them out. It also says the database keeps growing, points to the chat question 'What data is missing?' and gives FPR's website for a correction or a dataset to add.
values.3D + Time About tab: A short description (real terrain and building heights, and three clocks), a 'How to use it' list of five items, and 'Sources, licenses and how to cite' with the button 'Open the data dictionary'. It says the view uses public data, that most sources have an open license but some (the municipal transit feeds, the Junta de Planificación's maps) state none, and that the Data management page gives each file's license class.

name: Help buttons (?) beside layers and figures
plain: A round '?' button beside a layer, a tile or a chart opens a small box with a short explanation of what it shows and where it comes from.
definition: On the 2D map the box opens for the items listed below. The 3D view has 20 (2026-10-19): the layers it shares with the 2D map have the same help texts in both views (the six facility layers bring theirs with them, from core/facilities.js), except Municipal boundaries, whose 3D text points to the columns instead of the shading. On the Housing page each of the 28 variable blocks (a map and its ranked chart) has a '?' that shows the dataset's definition and its source reference. The other charts and tables on the Housing page have no '?'. A box closes with its close button, with Escape or with a click elsewhere. The texts are short summaries written into the page code. This dictionary gives the full account of each layer and variable.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the page is updated.

method: common.js (initHelp) opens a box for any element that carries a data-help key and looks the key up in a list: help.js (2D, loaded with its Spanish on the first press), core/facilities.js (the facility layers, both views, loaded with them), twin3d.js (3D) or housing.js (Housing page).
how_to_read: Read the box as a reminder. For a figure you plan to cite, use the dictionary entry.
caveats: The Tourism places help boxes (2D and 3D) call the classification 'the VIEWPR taxonomy'. This means the grouping of Overture categories into four tourism categories that Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) made. See the entry on classification.

name: Tourism places switch (2D map)
plain: Tourism places are the pins on the map: attractions, restaurants and bars, places to stay and visitor services listed by Overture Maps. Pins are coloured by category, and a dark ring marks a place inside a high-risk flood area mapped by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).
definition: The switch 'Tourism places' is off when the page opens, and the listings are not loaded yet. The label beside the switch says how much they weigh (about 3.0 MB compressed in Snapshot 2026-10, the listings and their transit access columns together). The first time you switch the layer on, download a municipality's places, search the listings or press 'Load the place listings' in the Municipality tab, the page fetches places.json and place_access.json. The pins are the listings in places.json that pass the current filters: the four category buttons, the minimum confidence slider and the places-of-worship switch. With the defaults the map counts 24,209 of the 32,541 listings in Snapshot 2026-10 (built 2026-10-02) and draws 23,467 of them as pins (holiday rentals are counted, not drawn), and the label beside the switch says how many are shown. Pins join into numbered clusters until zoom level 16. A click on a pin opens a card with the name, the type, the municipality and region, the street address when there is one, badges, links and a source line. The badges are listed below. Links go to the place's website, when it has one, and to OpenStreetMap at the place's location.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. Transit data are refreshed every night.

method: app.js (ensurePlaces, rebuildPlaces, placePopup) loads the listings on first use and makes one Leaflet marker for each visible place and groups the markers with Leaflet.markercluster: clusters of pins within 55 pixels, no clustering from zoom 16. Each pin is 26 pixels wide and carries the icon of the place type. When a filter changes, the pins are rebuilt in chunks of 4,000 so that the page stays responsive.
source_detail: places.json, Snapshot 2026-10: 32,541 listings, 24,209 of them on the default basis. Overture Maps Places release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026. Credit line on the map: 'Places © Overture Maps Foundation'.
how_to_read: A cluster number counts listings under the current filters. A pin is a listing, not a count of visitors or sales. The dark ring says the place's coordinates fall inside a mapped flood zone, not that the building floods. The Cite button of this entry cites the control. To cite the data, use the Cite button on the entries listed under Related, for example places.category.
caveats: Overture listings can be missing, duplicated, closed or out of date. The confidence slider filters them but does not remove every error.

The filters change the pins, the live numbers on the Municipality tab, the tourism results of the search box and the places download in comma-separated values (CSV) form. They do not change the statistics of each municipality (Rankings tab, shading, municipality download), which use the default filters: confidence 0.50 and no places of worship.

The badges come from point tests made when the data were built. The access class comes from the stored distances, which the nightly transit refresh can update. No badge is recalculated when you change a filter.

Until the listings are loaded, the Municipality tab shows the figures stored for the default filters, the search box offers to load them and the route planner leaves its tourism count out. Loading them is a download of about 3.0 MB compressed (Snapshot 2026-10), which matters on a phone or a slow connection.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Tourism places

values.Flood hazard area, zone <code>: The pin lies in a Special Flood Hazard Area. The badge prints the FEMA zone letter: AE, VE, AO, A or A99. It is a mapped hazard at a point, not an official flood determination (see the flood zone entry).
values.Zone X (0.2% annual chance): The pin lies in the lighter 0.2% annual chance zone. This is not a Special Flood Hazard Area.
values.Protected area: The badge gives the name of the protected area that holds the pin.
values.Transit access (class and distances): A badge names the place's access class: 'Frequent stop within 400 m', 'Stop within 400 m', 'Stop 400–800 m away', 'Only expired or unscheduled stops within 800 m' or 'No stop within 800 m'. Each badge has an icon as well as a colour, and hovering over it gives a note: the figures are schedule-based and in a straight line, a stop counts when its timetable has not ended, and real-time service, walking distance, públicos and taxis are not included. Under the badge, the line 'Nearest stop with a current timetable: <distance>' gives the distance and, within 400 m, the weekday departures and the Saturday and Sunday service. When a stop without a current timetable is closer than that stop, a line 'Any mapped stop (expired timetables and volunteer-mapped stops included): <distance>' follows, and hovering over it shows the stop's name. If the access file is missing or does not match the places file, the card shows only the badge 'any mapped stop <distance>'. The classes are described in methods.access_profile.
values.Confidence: Overture's confidence score for the listing, from 0 to 1.
values.Duplicates folded: How many duplicate listings were folded into the place.
values.Source line: Names Overture Maps, the contributing source and the original Overture category.

name: Category buttons (tourism places)
plain: Four buttons under the Tourism places switch turn each tourism category on or off: Attractions, Gastronomy, Accommodations and Visitor Services. All four are on when the page opens.
definition: Each button shows or hides every place of one category. A pressed button is on. A button that is off looks faded. The buttons change the pins, the live tiles and tables of the Municipality tab, the tourism results of the search box and the places file in comma-separated values (CSV) form. The 3D view has the same four buttons. The statistics of each municipality (Rankings tab, shading) do not follow the buttons. Pin and button colours: Attractions blue, Gastronomy green, Accommodations gold, Visitor Services red.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. Transit data are refreshed every night.

method: app.js (renderCatChips) keeps a set of the categories that are on and rebuilds the pins when a button is pressed. Colours and icons are defined once in icons.js. Pressing a button sets aria-pressed for screen readers.
how_to_read: A category is a group of Overture categories that Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) assigned. See the entry on classification for how the groups were made.
caveats: Places of Worship belong to Attractions, so they show only when the Attractions button and the worship switch are both on.
Colour is not the only cue. The pin icon and the type in the card also say what a place is.

name: Minimum confidence slider (tourism places)
plain: The 'Minimum confidence' slider hides tourism places that Overture rates below the chosen score. It starts at 0.50. Lower it to see more listings, or raise it to see fewer.
definition: Overture gives each listing a confidence score from 0 to 1, its estimate that the listing is a real, current place. The slider runs from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.05. The number beside it changes as you move the slider, and the map redraws when you let go. In Snapshot 2026-10 the scores run from 0.024 to 1.0. At 0.50 the map shows 24,209 places. At 0 it shows 27,509. Places of worship are left out of both counts. The slider also sets the live numbers on the Municipality tab, the tourism results of the search box and the places file in comma-separated values (CSV) form.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. Transit data are refreshed every night.

method: app.js keeps the value in S.conf. A place is visible when its confidence is at or above it, its category button is on and it is not a place of worship (unless the worship switch is on).
how_to_read: 0.50 is the observatory's own cut-off, not an Overture rule. In Snapshot 2026-10 it keeps 24,209 of the 27,509 listings (88%) that are not places of worship. A score is Overture's estimate, and a high score does not prove that a place is open today.
caveats: Only the 2D map has this slider. The 3D view, the route planner and the municipality statistics always use 0.50.
The slider does not change the numbers on the Rankings tab or in the shading. Those use the stored statistics.

The note under the slider on the page says 0.50 keeps 'the reliable majority'. The observatory has no test of reliability. 0.50 is a chosen cut-off, and the listings below it are not shown to be wrong.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Minimum confidence

name: Include places of worship switch
plain: 'Include places of worship' adds churches and other places of worship to the pins. It is off when the page opens, because most of them are not tourism supply.
definition: Places of worship are the listings of type 'Places of Worship', which belong to the Attractions category. The places file of Snapshot 2026-10 holds 5,032 of them, and 4,758 have a confidence score of 0.50 or more. With the switch off, none is drawn or counted. With it on, those that pass the other filters appear. Only the 2D map has this switch. The 3D view, the route planner, the municipality statistics and the Rankings tab always leave places of worship out.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. Transit data are refreshed every night.

method: app.js: a place is visible when the switch is on or its type is not 'Places of Worship'. The page's help text calls these places landmarks and heritage assets.
how_to_read: Turn the switch on to see landmarks such as churches on the map. Do not read them as visitor attractions in the statistics, because the statistics leave them out.
caveats: The listing does not say whether a place of worship is open to visitors.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Include places of worship

name: Flood zones switch (2D map)
plain: The 'Flood zones' switch shades the land that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) maps as flood-prone, from its National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL). It is off when the page opens. With it on, a click on the map tells you the FEMA zone at that point.
definition: The legend on the Map layers tab has four rows. Darkest blue is for V and VE zones (coastal high hazard, wave action). Mid blue is for A, AE, AH, AO and A99 zones (1% annual chance, the Special Flood Hazard Area). Red is for the regulatory floodway. Light blue is for the shaded X zone (0.2% annual chance). The first time you switch it on, the page downloads flood.geojson (about 8 MB in Snapshot 2026-10). With the switch on, a click adds a section 'Flood zone' to the popup, for up to two zones under the click, with a plain description (1% annual chance, 0.2% annual chance, or 'see FEMA zone definitions') and the zone subtype. The layer itself does not take clicks, so the municipality underneath still answers.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. Transit data are refreshed every night.

method: app.js (floodStyle, floodVisible, loadFlood, floodPopup). The 2D map draws a polygon when FEMA labels it as in the Special Flood Hazard Area or as the shaded 0.2% X zone. Minimal-hazard X, zone D and the labels OPEN WATER and AREA NOT INCLUDED are not drawn. Click answers use point-in-polygon tests on the same file (plan.js, featuresAt).
source_detail: flood.geojson. Credit line on the map: 'Flood zones: FEMA NFHL'.
how_to_read: Read the colour as the FEMA zone family, not as depth. An unshaded area is not proof of safety.
caveats: This is FEMA's mapped hazard at a location. It is not a forecast for any year and it says nothing about a building's elevation or insurance.
Drawn outlines are simplified. See the flood layer entry for the effect at zone edges.
If the file cannot be downloaded, the switch turns itself off.

This is a simplified copy of FEMA's data for context. FEMA's printed flood maps and Flood Insurance Study are the official designation. It is not a flood determination for any property. Read the source's terms before you rely on it.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Hazards and environment, Flood zones (FEMA)

name: Sea level rise switch and slider (2D map)
plain: The 'Sea level rise' switch shows a map from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) of land that would be flooded at the highest regular high tides if the sea rose by 1 to 10 feet. The slider picks the number of feet, and it starts at 3.
definition: The layer is off when the page opens. The slider runs from 1 to 10 feet in steps of 1. The label beside it says the chosen height, for example '3 ft'. When the layer is on, NOAA's tiles are drawn at 65% opacity. Moving the slider swaps the layer when you let go. The page address keeps the choice as slr=N. If NOAA does not answer, a message appears. The tiles are enlarged beyond zoom level 16. The page keeps no copy of the sea level data.

coverage.frequency: Live from NOAA each time the layer is shown.

method: app.js (setSlr, slrUrl) asks https://coast.noaa.gov/arcgis/rest/services/dc_slr/slr_{N}ft/MapServer for tiles, where N is the slider value.
source_detail: NOAA Office for Coastal Management, Sea Level Rise Viewer. Credit line on the map: 'Sea level rise: NOAA OCM'.
how_to_read: Read it as a what-if for planning: 'land that would be wet at this height'. It is not a timeline and it names no year.
caveats: The page calls this a what-if for planning, not a timeline. NOAA says the layer shows water at the highest high tides and does not model storm surge, erosion, subsidence or new construction. NOAA calls it a planning reference that should not be used for navigation, permitting or other legal purposes.
If NOAA changes or removes the service, the layer stops working. The observatory cannot restore it.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Sea level rise, 5 ft

name: Transit routes switch (2D map)
plain: The 'Transit routes' switch draws every public route in the observatory's data. These are the Tren Urbano, buses and ferries of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI, the Integrated Transport Authority), municipal buses and trolleys, and routes mapped in OpenStreetMap. Thicker lines have more weekday trips.
definition: Width grows with the weekday trips of the route, from 2 to 7 pixels. The Tren Urbano is one pixel wider than a bus line with the same trips. Routes mapped in OpenStreetMap are 2.5 pixels wide and ferries 3. Pointing at a line thickens it. A click opens a card with the route name, the operator and network, weekday, Saturday and Sunday trips, the first and last weekday departure, how the line was drawn, the state of the timetable with its dates, and a credit line. The routes load from transit_routes.geojson (about 1.0 MB in Snapshot 2026-10) the first time the switch is on. The colours and line styles are listed below.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time. Files are rewritten only when a feed changes. The OpenStreetMap routes (16 in Snapshot 2026-10) are refreshed only by a full build. The nightly job keeps the last copy.

method: app.js (loadRoutes) and network.js (routeColor, routeStyle, routePopup). width = 2 + 0.7 x log2(1 + weekday trips), at most 7. The 'Show' button of an operator on the Transit tab dims every other operator's lines to 12% opacity.
source_detail: transit_routes.geojson. Timetable feeds are in the General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) format. Credit line on the map: 'Routes: ATI, municipal GTFS feeds, OpenStreetMap'.
how_to_read: Read a line as a guide to where a route runs. Open its card to see whether its timetable is current, expiring or expired.
caveats: Routes of operators whose timetable has expired stay on the map.
A route in a feed is not proof that the service runs today.
In Snapshot 2026-10, the 16 routes from OpenStreetMap have no timetable, so their trip counts are 0, meaning none published.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Transit routes

values.ATI buses: Blue line. It includes the buses of the Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses (AMA, the Metropolitan Bus Authority), Metrobús and Metro Urbano.
values.Routes mapped in OpenStreetMap: Gold dashes. In Snapshot 2026-10 there are 16 routes that volunteers mapped: 9 carros públicos and 7 bus or trolley lines. None has a timetable.
values.Solid line: The line follows the operator's own route shape or the road network.
values.Dashed, lighter line: The feed lists the stops out of order, so the visiting order was inferred.
values.Dotted line: No road path was found, so the line joins the stops straight.

name: Transit stops switch (2D map and 3D view)
plain: The 'Transit stops' switch shows boarding points: scheduled stops from the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and from municipal timetable feeds in General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) form, plus bus stops that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap. The number beside the switch counts them.
definition: The layer holds the points of kind transit_stop (scheduled stops, 3,781 in Snapshot 2026-10) and bus_stop (OpenStreetMap stops that are not within 30 metres of a scheduled stop, 459), 4,240 in all. The 3,781 are the scheduled stops that are not stations. In Snapshot 2026-10 there are 3,847 scheduled stops in all. The other 66 are bus stations, ferry terminals and Tren Urbano stations, and they appear on the stations layer. The first time you switch it on, the page downloads transport.json (about 1.3 MB in Snapshot 2026-10), which the stations and taxi layers share. Points join into numbered blue clusters until zoom 15. A click opens a card with the stop's name, kind and municipality, the routes and modes that call there, weekday departures, a weekend line ('Weekend departures: Saturday N · Sunday N', with 'none listed' for a day that has no departures, or 'No weekend departures in the published timetable' when neither day has any; scheduled stops only), the end date of the stop's timetable ('Timetable valid until' a date, or 'Timetable ended' with a warning sign when the date has passed), the operator, a note when the source says wheelchair boarding is possible, and a source line. The 400 m walk rings use these points. The 3D view has the same switch, in the same group: the same points, in blue clusters that give their count up to zoom 14 and as single dots from zoom 15, with the same card (a click on a cluster zooms in).

coverage.frequency: Scheduled stops are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time. OpenStreetMap points are read at each full build.

method: app.js (loadTransport) and twin3d.js (addStops); the card is transportPopup in access.js, which both views load. The clusters group points within 40 pixels, in both views.
source_detail: transport.json (kinds transit_stop and bus_stop). Credit line on the map: 'Stops: ATI GTFS · © OpenStreetMap contributors'.
how_to_read: Check the source line first. A scheduled stop appears in a published timetable. An OpenStreetMap stop only shows that someone mapped a stop there.
caveats: Stops of operators whose timetable has expired stay on the map.
OpenStreetMap stops can be missing, out of date or wrong. The observatory does not check them on the ground.

The credit line on the map names ATI and OpenStreetMap only. In Snapshot 2026-10, 2,381 of the 3,781 scheduled stops come from municipal feeds, so credit both when you cite. The stop card's type label reads 'Transit stop (ATI)' for every scheduled stop, municipal ones included. The source line at the bottom of the card names the actual feed.

The card says 'wheelchair accessible' only when the source states that boarding is possible (feed field wheelchair_boarding = 1, or OpenStreetMap tag wheelchair=yes). Stops without the note are unknown or not stated, not inaccessible. In Snapshot 2026-10, none of the 1,400 ATI scheduled stops carries the note. In the feed standard, value 1 means that some vehicles can be boarded, not all. The note is not an accessibility audit.
The card compares the timetable end date with the date on your device. For a stop of an operator whose timetable has ended, it still shows the departures that the old timetable lists.

The weekend line shows what the published timetable lists. Many feeds list no weekend departures at all (in the 2026-10 snapshot only 3 of the 18 current feeds list Saturday departures and 1 lists Sunday departures), so 'none listed' often means that the feed does not cover weekends, not that there is no service.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Transit stops (zoom in to see points)
3D view, Layers tab: switch on Transit stops (Santurce, San Juan)

name: Stations, terminals and airports switch (2D map and 3D view)
plain: The 'Stations, terminals & airports' switch shows the larger mobility points: bus stations and terminals, Tren Urbano stations, ferry terminals and airports.
definition: The layer holds 145 points in Snapshot 2026-10: 91 bus stations and terminals, 16 Tren Urbano stations, 13 ferry terminals and 25 airports and airfields (14 from the list of the Federal Aviation Administration, FAA, and 11 from OpenStreetMap). Icons are larger than stop icons and are not clustered. A click opens the same card as a stop. For an airport the card also says 'Public use' or 'Private use' and gives its codes. The layer is off when the page opens. The 3D view has the same switch: the same points as dots (Tren Urbano red, ferry terminals teal, bus stations and airports charcoal, airports larger), with the same card.

coverage.frequency: Scheduled stations are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time. OpenStreetMap points and FAA airports are read at each full build.

method: app.js (loadTransport) and twin3d.js (addHubs): points whose kind is bus_station, rail_station, ferry_terminal or airport go to this layer. The card is transportPopup in access.js, which both views load.
source_detail: transport.json (kinds bus_station, rail_station, ferry_terminal and airport). Timetable data are from the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and municipal feeds in General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) form. Credit line on the map: 'Stations: ATI GTFS, OpenStreetMap, FAA'.
how_to_read: Use it to see where the main interchange and entry points are. An airport is not a transit stop.
caveats: In Snapshot 2026-10, the card says 'Public use' for every airport that is not marked private. That includes 11 airports from OpenStreetMap, which carry no public-use flag. Only the 14 FAA records state it (10 public use, 4 private use). The names of some OpenStreetMap airfields say closed, historic or military, and one includes 'CERRADO' (closed). The municipality chip counts only FAA airports marked public use, so the chip and the card can differ. Treat OpenStreetMap airfields as mapped, not confirmed open.
A station from OpenStreetMap shows that someone mapped it, not that it is staffed or served today.

The credit line on the map names the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI), OpenStreetMap and the FAA. In Snapshot 2026-10, 29 bus stations come from municipal feeds, so credit those feeds too when you cite.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Stations, terminals & airports
3D view, Layers tab: switch on Stations, terminals & airports

name: Taxi stands and EV charging switch (2D map and 3D view)
plain: The 'Taxi stands & EV charging' switch shows taxi stands and electric vehicle (EV) chargers that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap. There are 9 taxi stands and 11 chargers in Snapshot 2026-10.
definition: The layer reads points of kind taxi, ev_charging, bike_rental and helipad. Snapshot 2026-10 holds only taxi stands and chargers. Click for a card with the name, the kind and the municipality. Ride-hailing is not drawn here. Whether Uber lists a municipality is a yes or no, shown by shading the map by 'Uber lists service' or by the chip on the Municipality tab. The 3D view has the same switch and card; its dots take the colour of their kind (taxi stands amber, chargers green).

coverage.frequency: Read at each full build.

method: app.js (loadTransport) and twin3d.js (addTaxi): kinds in TAXI_KINDS (access.js) go to this layer.
source_detail: transport.json. Credit line on the map: '© OpenStreetMap contributors'.
how_to_read: Use it to see where such points are known. It is not a list of all taxis or chargers.
caveats: OpenStreetMap volunteers add these points, so the layer shows what has been mapped (9 taxi stands and 11 chargers in Snapshot 2026-10), not what exists.
Taxi stands and chargers are not scheduled transit and are not counted in the stop totals.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Taxi stands & EV charging
3D view, Layers tab: switch on Taxi stands & EV charging

name: 400 m walk radius switch (2D map and 3D view)
plain: 'Show 400 m walk radius around stops' draws a circle of 400 metres around each stop, bus station, Tren Urbano station and ferry terminal. The circles appear only when you are zoomed in and the stops or stations layer is on.
definition: 400 metres is about a quarter mile, a common planning distance for walking to a stop. It is a choice made for the observatory, not a measure of how far people walk. The rings are thin blue circles with a very light blue fill and a 400 m radius, drawn in Snapshot 2026-10 for 4,360 points (the 4,240 stops and the 120 stations and terminals, airports excluded). They show when the switch is on, the map zoom is 14 or higher, and 'Transit stops' or 'Stations, terminals & airports' is on. If only one of those two layers is on, the rings of both kinds still appear. Rings overlap where stops are close. The same distance defines 'within 400 m of any mapped stop' and 'within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable' in the statistics. The 3D view has the same switch, under the same conditions: the rings lie flat on the ground with a radius of 400 metres at every zoom (a MapLibre circle whose radius in pixels doubles at each zoom level, set from each point's latitude), and the chip counts them while they are drawn.

coverage.frequency: Scheduled stops are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time.

method: app.js (updateRings): ringLayer holds one circle for each point of kind transit_stop, bus_stop, bus_station, rail_station and ferry_terminal. twin3d.js (addRings, updateRings) draws the same points in the 3D view.
how_to_read: Look at what the circles cover and what they leave out. Places outside every circle are more than 400 m, in a straight line, from the nearest stop.
caveats: The distance is a straight line. It ignores rivers, hills, fences and the street pattern.
Rings include stops of expired timetables and OpenStreetMap stops that have no timetable.
The rings say nothing about how often or when a vehicle comes.

A place inside a ring can still have no stop with a current timetable within 400 m: the ring may belong to a stop whose timetable has ended or to a volunteer-mapped stop. The place's pop-up gives its access class.

view.label: 2D map: 400 m rings at Santurce, San Juan
3D view: switch on Transit stops and the 400 m rings (Santurce, San Juan)

source_detail: transport.json, Snapshot 2026-10: 4,360 points of kind transit_stop, bus_stop, bus_station, rail_station and ferry_terminal. The stops come from timetable feeds of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and of municipalities in General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) form, and from OpenStreetMap. The rings carry no credit line of their own. The stops or stations layer that must be on shows its own credit line: see the entries on those two layers.

name: Protected areas switch (2D map)
plain: The 'Protected areas' switch shades the protected areas of the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US) of the US Geological Survey (USGS), from national forests to local parks. It holds 665 records in Snapshot 2026-10. Records overlap, so this is not a count of separate areas. The switch is off when the page opens.
definition: Areas are drawn in green at 30% opacity. With the switch on, a click adds a section to the popup for up to two protected areas under the click. It gives the name, the designation (in Snapshot 2026-10 the data hold 22 codes: the card spells out 10 of them, for example National Forest or Local Park, and shows the raw code for the other 12, such as SCA, SRMA and MIL, which covers 126 of the 665 records), the manager, the public access (open access, restricted access, closed or unknown), the acres and the Gap Analysis Project (GAP) status. The GAP status is a rating from 1 to 4 of how strictly the land is managed for nature. The first time you switch it on, the page downloads protected.geojson (about 1.5 MB in Snapshot 2026-10).

coverage.frequency: PAD-US 4.1, downloaded for each snapshot.

method: app.js (protStyle, protPopup, padTxt, loadProt). The codes are spelled out with the lists in the PAD constant, taken from the PAD-US data dictionary.
source_detail: protected.geojson. Credit line on the map: 'Protected areas: USGS PAD-US'.
how_to_read: Check the designation and the GAP status before you read a patch as a nature reserve.
caveats: 'Protected' has a wide meaning here. It includes recreation areas, local parks and military land.
Overlapping areas are stacked, so a darker patch can be several records.

In Snapshot 2026-10 the card spells out the designation for 539 of the 665 records. For the other 126 records (codes such as SCA, SRMA and MIL) it shows the raw PAD-US code. Look the code up in the entry on the designation. A military area, for example, shows only 'MIL'.

In Snapshot 2026-10 two thirds of the records (440 of 665) have GAP status 4, which the card words as 'no known biodiversity mandate'. Read the GAP status before you treat a patch as a nature reserve.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Protected areas

name: Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 switch (2D map)
plain: The 'Land use 2015' switch shades the whole island by the Junta de Planificación's land-use plan: urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural and specially protected rural land. It is off when the page opens.
definition: The legend has ten rows with their colours. Suelo Urbano (urban) is gray. Urbanizable programado (planned growth) is orange. Urbanizable no programado (reserve growth) is light gold. Rústico común (ordinary rural) is light green. Rústico especialmente protegido (protected rural) is green. The five special protection classes (ecological, agricultural, hydric, ecological and hydric, agricultural and hydric) are dark green, lime and blues. Other protection combinations in the data use the colour stored in the file. Water and road polygons are not drawn. Polygons are drawn at 50% opacity. A click adds a section to the popup with the class name, the class code and the municipio of the first polygon under the click. The first time you switch it on, the page downloads landuse.geojson (about 17.7 MB in Snapshot 2026-10), the largest file of the map. A note under the legend says that zoning districts (Calificación) are not shown, because the Junta's service did not answer when Snapshot 2026-10 was built. Since 2026-10-16 every class of the legend has a tick box, ticked when the layer opens: unticking a class hides it on the map and in the click pop-up. The button above the legend opens the land-use analysis (layers.landuse_analysis).

coverage.frequency: A single plan version, dated 30 November 2015.

method: app.js (loadLanduse, landusePopup). The layer filters out the groups water and road. Colours are stored in the file.
source_detail: landuse.geojson. File version label: 'PUT-2014, 30-NOV-2015', the plan of 30 November 2015, which the page calls Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015. Credit line on the map: 'Land use: Junta de Planificación'.
how_to_read: Use it for the broad pattern of where the plan allows growth and where it protects land.
caveats: The plan is a classification for planning. It is not a zoning map and does not say what may be built on a lot.
The plan dates from 2015. Land may since have been built on, reclassified or protected.
Polygons are simplified, so do not use the layer to decide the class of one lot.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015

name: Municipal boundaries switch (2D map and 3D view), labels and hover box (2D map)
plain: The 'Municipal boundaries' switch draws the outlines of the 78 municipalities. It is on when the page opens. Pointing at a municipality shows a short summary, and a click opens its profile.
definition: Outlines are blue lines. Names appear from zoom level 10. Pointing at a municipality (with a mouse) thickens its outline and shows a box with its name, its number of tourism places, the share of those places in a flood hazard area and its 2020 population. A click opens the Municipality tab and outlines the municipality in red. When a flood, protected-area, land-use or barrio layer is on and has a feature under the click, the popup comes first, with a link 'Open the <name> profile'. When the switch is off, a click no longer selects a municipality and the outlines and names disappear. The 3D view has the same switch, on when it opens and never counted, as on the 2D map: it shows or hides the outlines only (no labels, no hover box), and a click on a municipality opens its card with the outlines on or off. When a flood zone, protected area, land-use class, Comunidad Especial or barrio is under the click, the card of those areas comes first, with the same link 'Open the <name> profile', which opens the municipality's card.

coverage.frequency: Outline shapes are the Census Bureau's generalized layer, January 1, 2023 vintage, cut at the shoreline. Population is the 2020 Census count. Counts are rebuilt with each snapshot.

method: app.js (init, muniStyle, selectMuni). In the 3D view, twin3d.js draws the outlines (muni-line) and the switch lyMuni shows or hides them.
source_detail: municipios.geojson and municipalities.json. Credit line on the map: 'Boundaries & population: US Census 2020'.
how_to_read: Use the outline to see which municipality a place is in. The summary box counts places with the default filters.
caveats: Outlines are generalized shoreline-clipped shapes. Do not use them to decide whether a lot lies inside a municipality.
Cite the outlines as the Census Bureau's generalized boundaries as of January 1, 2023, cut at the shoreline. Only the population is a 2020 count.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Boundaries
3D view, Layers tab: Territory, Municipal boundaries

name: Barrios switch (2D map and 3D view)
plain: The 'Barrios' switch draws the 901 barrios of the Census Bureau's January 2023 layer, the districts inside each municipality, as dashed outlines. Click inside one for its counts.
definition: Barrios are dashed blue outlines. The layer is off when the page opens. The first time you switch it on, the page downloads barrios.geojson (about 1.0 MB in Snapshot 2026-10). With the switch on, a click adds a section to the popup. It gives the barrio's name, its municipality and its area in square kilometres. It also gives the number of tourism places, the places per square kilometre, how many of those places are in a flood hazard area, and how many are within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable (and how many of those are near a frequent stop) and within 400 m of any mapped stop. The 3D view has the same switch: the same dashed outlines and, for a click inside a barrio, the same section, last in the card after the other areas under the click, as on the 2D map.

coverage.frequency: Outline shapes are the Census Bureau's generalized county-subdivision layer, January 1, 2023 vintage, cut at the shoreline. Counts are rebuilt with each snapshot.

method: app.js (loadBarrios), twin3d.js (addBarrios) and access.js (barrioPopup, shared by both views). The counts are stored in barrios.geojson.
source_detail: barrios.geojson. Credit line on the map: 'Barrios: US Census Bureau'.
how_to_read: Compare barrios by places per square kilometre, not by raw counts, because their areas differ a great deal.
caveats: A barrio is a Census statistical unit. It is not a neighbourhood or an electoral unit.
Barrio names repeat across municipalities. Read the municipality in the popup.

Barrio counts use the default filters (confidence 0.50, no places of worship). The confidence slider, the category buttons and the worship switch do not change them. The counts are rebuilt only at a full build, so between full builds they can lag the municipality figures.
Cite the outlines as the Census Bureau's generalized county-subdivision boundaries as of January 1, 2023, cut at the shoreline.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Barrios (Bayamón area)
3D view, Layers tab: switch on Barrios (Bayamón area)

name: Click on the 2D map: what opens
plain: A click on the 2D map opens a popup for the overlays that are on at that spot. If no overlay has anything there, a click on a municipality opens its profile.
definition: In this order, the popup can hold: up to two flood zones, up to two protected areas, the land-use class of one polygon (water and road polygons are skipped), and one barrio. If the boundaries layer is on and the click is inside a municipality, a link 'Open the <name> profile' is added. If no overlay has a feature at the point, the click selects the municipality (when Boundaries is on) and opens the Municipality tab. Pins, stops, routes and vehicle dots have their own popups. Two modes take the click away: choosing a point for the route planner, and having the Analysis tab open with at least one visible layer. In the second case the click opens the economy popup for the municipality.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the page is updated.

method: app.js (the map click handler) with featuresAt in plan.js. Overlays are not interactive, so a polygon layer cannot swallow clicks meant for the municipality below it.
how_to_read: Switch on the overlays you want to read before you click.
caveats: The popup shows up to two flood zones and two protected areas. A point with more overlapping records shows only the first ones.

view.label: 2D map

name: Shade municipalities by (2D map, retired)
plain: A menu of the 2D map that coloured the 78 municipalities by one of 35 measures. It was retired on 2026-11-05 (navigation plan, decision 81): each measure is now a dataset, shaded from Explore, the Catalog or Rankings, and an old link with s=<field> opens the same measure as that dataset.
definition: app.js SHADE_DS lists the 35 fields the menu had and the dataset each now opens, with its scale where the menu used one (tourism places per 1,000 residents or per square kilometre). An address with s=<field> is read when the data of the Analysis tab load (economy.js econInit): the dataset is shaded in five classes, the tab does not change, and the address is rewritten with e=. Eleven of the fields became datasets for this (core/adapters.js SNAPSHOT_FIELDS): nine shares of tourism places near transit, the change in median gross rent since 2008-2012 and Uber's listing (1 or 0).

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot (Snapshot 2026-10). The measures use different years: tourism places and flood exposure 2026; population 2020 Census; housing measures American Community Survey (ACS) 2020-2024, with the rent change starting from the 2008-2012 window; land use plan of 30 November 2015; residents served 2020 census blocks against the stops of the latest build; the access shares of places as of the date in access_as_of; the Uber list checked 2026-10-01. Transit data are refreshed every night.

method: app.js SHADE_DS; economy.js econInit; core/adapters.js SNAPSHOT_FIELDS. tests/test_catalog.py checks that every one of the 35 fields opens a dataset.
how_to_read: Read the dataset the measure now opens: its legend, its scale and its own dictionary entry.
caveats: The three 'places shown' measures counted only the places the filters let through; their dataset counts every tourism place.
'Population 2020' opens the population dataset, which shows its latest year.
The 14 municipalities with no mapped transit stop have no value for the transit shares of places, not 0%: there is no measurement.

values.assets: Tourism places. Count of places in Snapshot 2026-10 (confidence 0.50 or more, no places of worship).
values.assets_per_1000_residents: Places per 1,000 residents. Places divided by 2020 Census residents, times 1,000.
values.assets_per_km2: Places per km². Places divided by land area in square kilometres.
values.sfha_pct: % of places in flood hazard area. Share of the municipality's places inside a Special Flood Hazard Area.
values.in_sfha: Places in flood hazard area. Count of places.
values.in_protected: Places inside protected areas. Count of places.
values.with_website: Places with a website. Count of places.
values.acc_cur400_pct: % of places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable. The nearest stop with a published timetable (ATI, the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, or a municipal system, in a feed that has not ended) is 400 m or less away in a straight line. Municipalities with no stop counted are left unshaded.
values.acc_freq400_pct: % of places within 400 m of a frequent stop (20+ weekday departures). A stop with a current timetable and 20 or more departures on a typical weekday is 400 m or less away. Municipalities with no stop counted are left unshaded.
values.acc_sat400_pct: % of places within 400 m of a stop with Saturday service. A stop with a current timetable and at least one Saturday departure in the published timetable is 400 m or less away. Municipalities with no stop counted are left unshaded.
values.acc_sun400_pct: % of places within 400 m of a stop with Sunday service. A stop with a current timetable and at least one Sunday departure in the published timetable is 400 m or less away. Municipalities with no stop counted are left unshaded.
values.acc_paper_pct: % of places near only an expired or unscheduled stop. A mapped stop is 400 m or less away but none with a current timetable: its timetable has ended, or volunteers mapped it and there is none. Municipalities with no stop counted are left unshaded.
values.transit_pct: % of places within 400 m of any mapped stop. The nearest stop, station or terminal of any kind is 400 m or less away in a straight line, including stops whose timetable has ended and stops that volunteers mapped. Municipalities with no stop counted are left unshaded.
values.transit_stops: Transit stops and stations. Count of scheduled stops, OpenStreetMap bus stops, bus stations, Tren Urbano stations and ferry terminals inside the municipality. Airports, taxi stands and electric vehicle chargers are not counted.
values.uber_listed: Uber lists service (yes or no). Two colours: listed or not listed. It is a hand-typed copy of Uber's Puerto Rico cities page checked 2026-10-01 (57 of 78 municipalities listed). A listing, not measured coverage. 'Not listed' does not mean Uber is absent, because Uber says its service reaches beyond the places it lists.
values.affordability_ratio: Housing: affordability ratio. Median home value divided by the largest 30-year loan a household with the median income can carry (30% of income for housing, 78% of that for principal and interest, 5% rate). name: Municipality tab (profile of one municipality)
plain: The Municipality tab is a one-page profile of one municipality: tourism places, flood and protected-area exposure, transit access, housing and land use. Click a municipality on the map, or pick one in the search box or the Rankings tab.
definition: The tab opens when you click a municipality on the map, pick one in the search box or the Rankings tab, or follow a link such as index.html#San%20Juan. The first block is headed 'Visitor economy'. Once the tourism place listings are loaded, its tiles are counted from the places the map is showing, so they follow the category buttons, the confidence slider and the worship switch. Before that (the listings are not part of the first load) the tiles show the figures stored for the default filters, a line says so and offers a button 'Load the place listings', and the top types and the list of places in a flood hazard area wait for the listings. Places per 1,000 residents and per square kilometre are the stored values, which use the default filters. The rank line uses the stored values too. The housing section is headed 'ACS 2024', the 2020-2024 window of the American Community Survey (ACS). The parts of the tab are listed below.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. Transit data are refreshed every night.

method: app.js (selectMuni, renderMuni). The rank line uses the stored assets and sfha_pct fields.
how_to_read: Compare a tile with the same tile for other municipalities, not with a target. Read the housing figures as survey estimates.
caveats: Tiles that follow the filters can differ from the stored statistics when you change a filter. The rank line ignores your filters and says so.
The housing tiles are survey estimates. Their margins of error are large in small municipalities, and this tab does not show them. The Housing page does.
The Uber chip is a yes or no from Uber's own cities page. It does not show that a driver is nearby.

In Snapshot 2026-10, the airport chip counts as public only the 10 airports of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) that are marked public use. The card on the stations layer says 'Public use' for 21 airports: those 10 and 11 airports from OpenStreetMap that carry no flag. See the entry on the stations layer.

Without the place listings the tiles show the stored figures for the default filters (confidence 0.50 or higher, no places of worship). In Snapshot 2026-10 they agree with the tiles counted from the listings for every municipality.

view.label: 2D map: Municipality tab for Ponce

values.Header: The municipality's name, its tourism region, its residents (2020 Census) and its land area in square kilometres.
values.Tourism tiles: Tourism places, the share in a flood hazard area, places per 1,000 residents, places per square kilometre, places inside protected areas and places with a website.
values.Mobility tiles: There are up to five mobility tiles. The first two are shares of the places shown and appear when the access file has loaded: places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable, and places with frequent service (20+ weekday departures). The third is the share of the places shown within 400 m of any mapped stop. The first three tiles show a dash when the municipality has no stop counted. The fourth is the number of stops and stations. The fifth is the share of residents within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable (the share for any scheduled stop, expired timetables included, if the field is missing). A line under the tiles gives the stops by state: 'Stops: N with a current timetable · N with an expired timetable · N mapped by volunteers (no timetable)'.
values.Tile colours: Three tiles change colour. The flood tile warns when more than 25% of the places shown are in a flood hazard area. The residents-served tile warns when fewer than 25% of residents live within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable. The affordability tile warns when the ratio, rounded to two decimals, is above 1, and is green otherwise. These are the observatory's own signals, not standards. The tile for places inside protected areas is always green.
values.Chips: Tren Urbano stations, bus stations, ferry terminals, airports (with the number open to the public), scheduled stops, taxi stands, electric vehicle (EV) charging points, the state of the municipal bus schedule, and whether Uber lists the municipality.
values.Rank line: The rank among the 78 by tourism places and by share in a flood hazard area, with the default filters. It ignores your filters and says so.
values.Housing section: Headed 'ACS 2024'. It shows the affordability ratio, the median home value and rent, the share of renters who are cost-burdened and the share of seasonal or recreational units.
values.Land use line: The shares of land that are urban, urbanizable and especially protected (Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015), with a link to the full profile on the Housing page.
values.Lists and buttons: Bars by category, the eight most common place types, and a list of up to 60 places inside a flood hazard area (click a row to fly to the place). Two buttons download the shown places as a comma-separated values (CSV) file and zoom to the municipality.

name: Rankings tab
plain: The Rankings tab lists the 78 municipalities in order of one measure, highest first. Pick the measure from the menu, reverse the order with a click, and download the whole municipality table as a comma-separated values (CSV) file.
definition: The menu 'Rank municipalities by' has 26 options, listed below with the field they read. It starts on 'Tourism places'. The table has the rank, the municipality and the value, and a second column with the number of tourism places (not shown when you rank by tourism places). Only municipalities with a value are listed. A click on the column title reverses the order, and the arrow shows the direction. A click on a row selects the municipality and opens the Municipality tab. Numbers are rounded: whole numbers for counts and most percentages, one decimal for places per 1,000 residents, places per square kilometre and the seasonal share, and two decimals for the affordability ratio. The button 'Download municipality table (CSV)' saves one row per municipality.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot (Snapshot 2026-10). The measures use different years: see the codes below and the entry on shading. Transit data are refreshed every night.

method: app.js (renderRank, downloadCsv). The table is built from the stored statistics, so it does not follow the category buttons, the confidence slider or the worship switch.
how_to_read: Rank 1 is the highest value, not the best result. Compare ranks only within one measure.
caveats: Tied values get consecutive ranks. Their order follows the order of the municipalities in the data file.

In Snapshot 2026-10, 14 municipalities have no stop counted inside their border. They are left out of the ranking by the share of places within 400 m of any mapped stop and by the five access shares (a stop with a current timetable, a frequent stop, Saturday service, Sunday service and only an expired or unscheduled stop).
The table rounds. For citation, use the stored values in the download.
A percentage of places can swing widely where a municipality has few places. In Snapshot 2026-10 the smallest has 36, so one place is 2.8 points. Check the count of places before you compare shares.

Transit stops and stations counts every mapped stop, station and terminal, including OpenStreetMap stops and stops of expired timetables. It reflects mapping and stop density, not how often vehicles run.

The rent change is not adjusted for inflation. In Snapshot 2026-10, 76 municipalities have a rise, and 52 of them rose by less than US consumer prices (36.6% from 2012 to 2024), so by that measure they had a fall in real terms.

name: Transit tab: summary figures and 'Show transit only'
plain: The top of the Transit tab shows four figures. Two count operators: those that publish a schedule and those that publish none. One counts the routes on the map. One gives the share of residents who live within 400 metres of a scheduled stop.
definition: The first figure counts operators whose timetable is current, expiring or expired, with the three counts in brackets. The second counts operators with no public schedule data. The third is the number of routes on the map (165 in Snapshot 2026-10). The fourth divides the residents within 400 m of a scheduled stop, summed over the municipalities, by all residents, and adds the same share counting only operators whose timetable has not expired. The state of each operator is worked out in your browser from the end date of its timetable and today's date in Puerto Rico, so the counts can differ from those on the build date. The button 'Show transit only on the map' switches tourism places off and transit routes on. Other layers stay as they are.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time. The counts of operator states are recalculated each time the page opens.

method: network.js (renderNetSummary). Residents come from the coverage records of operators.json, which use 2020 Census blocks.
how_to_read: Read the last figure as a share of residents near a stop in a straight line. It does not say how often vehicles come.
caveats: An operator with no feed may still run service. 'No public schedule' means no timetable data were found.
Stops of expired timetables count in the first residents figure. The second figure leaves them out.

name: Transit tab: What is live
plain: The 'What is live' box says that real-time bus positions are not available to the public and lists what exists, with a status for each source and a link.
definition: The box opens with 'Real-time bus positions are not available to the public' and the date of the check. Below it each source has a coloured status and a one-line detail. There are six sources in Snapshot 2026-10: the real-time feed of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI), the Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses (AMA) Móvil app, ATI express buses, municipal systems, the AcuaExpreso ferries and aircraft near Puerto Rico.

coverage.frequency: Last checked 2026-10-02.

method: network.js (renderLiveStatus) reads the live list of operators.json. Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) enters the statuses by hand after each check. The observatory does not test the sources automatically.
how_to_read: Where the observatory shows vehicles moving, it replays a timetable. See 'Vehicles on their timetable now'.
caveats: The check is a snapshot. A feed published after the check date is not shown until the list is updated.

name: Transit tab: Operators list
plain: The Operators list names every transit operator in the observatory and the state of its public timetable: current, expiring, expired or none. Press 'Show' to highlight an operator's routes on the map.
definition: In Snapshot 2026-10 the list has 44 operators. The menu 'Show' filters it (see the codes below). Each row has a coloured dot for the type of operator, a short name with a status pill, and the full name. A line of details gives the routes, stops, weekday trips and the last date of the timetable. It adds flags such as 'no route shapes (drawn along roads)' and 'N routes list stops out of order'. An operator with no timetable feed (a General Transit Feed Specification, or GTFS, file) shows 'No GTFS feed found' (or 'Públicos run without a published schedule') and, when it has one, its number in the federal National Transit Database. 'Show' switches the routes layer on, dims every other operator's lines and zooms to that operator. Press it again to clear. An operator without routes but with a municipality has an 'Open <municipality>' button. The codes below give the filter menu, the status pills and the operator types, with their counts on 4 October 2026.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time. States are recalculated each time the page opens.

method: network.js (opStatus, renderOpList, highlightOperator). The state is recalculated from the feed's end date every time the page opens. Expired means the end date has passed. Expiring means 60 days or fewer remain. States other than these three come from the stored file.
how_to_read: A current state means the timetable's dates cover today. It does not mean service runs as planned.
caveats: The state is judged from one date in the feed. A feed can be out of date in practice while its end date is still ahead.
Operators in none of the sources the observatory reads are not listed.

name: Vehicles on their timetable now switch (Transit tab)
plain: 'Vehicles on their timetable now' draws a dot for each scheduled vehicle that should be in service at this moment, in Puerto Rico time. It replays timetables. It is not tracking by Global Positioning System (GPS).
definition: The switch is off when the page opens. When it is on, the dots update every 5 seconds. The map picks the Sunday, Saturday or weekday file for today in Puerto Rico. A dot is red for the Tren Urbano, teal for ferries, blue for buses of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and green for municipal buses. Pointing at a dot names the route and the operator and repeats that the position is not GPS. A note under the switch gives the number of vehicles, the day type, the time, and the six operators with the most vehicles. Trips of operators whose timetable has expired are left out. Holidays are not modelled. The first time you switch it on, the page downloads the timetable file for the day type (the weekday file is about 2.2 MB in Snapshot 2026-10).

coverage.frequency: Timetables are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time. Positions are recalculated every 5 seconds.

method: network.js (updateNow, setNow). A trip is in service when the time lies between its first and last stop time. Its position is worked out between the two stops around the current time, in proportion to the time elapsed.
how_to_read: Read a dot as where the schedule says a vehicle is, not where it is.
caveats: No public real-time bus feed exists, so a late or cancelled vehicle is shown as on time.

The position follows the route line between stops at an even speed. A trip whose stops fit no line of its route (106 of 3,297 weekday trips in Snapshot 2026-10) moves in a straight line, so its dot can sit off the road.
Operators with no published timetable, públicos and OpenStreetMap routes are absent.

In Snapshot 2026-10, on Saturday only 4 operators have a timetable file (ATI, Guaynabo, Juncos and Vega Alta). On Sunday only ATI does, so municipal buses are absent on those days even where they run.

A dot moves between the stops that have a scheduled time. In Snapshot 2026-10, 532 of the 3,297 weekday trips list only their first and last stop; 523 of them still follow their route line, so their dots keep to the road, but the time in between is spread evenly.

view.label: 2D map: Vehicles on their timetable now

source_detail: Snapshot 2026-10: trips.json (weekday, 3,297 trips), trips_sa.json (Saturday, 1,648 trips) and trips_su.json (Sunday, 381 trips). The vehicle dots carry no credit line of their own. Name ATI and the municipal operators when you cite.

name: Residents far from service switch (2D Transit tab and 3D Route tab)
plain: 'Residents far from service' draws a circle for each census block with at least 40 residents whose nearest scheduled stop is more than 800 metres away. Bigger circles mean more residents.
definition: The switch is off when the page opens. The layer has 14,405 circles in Snapshot 2026-10 (distances walked along mapped roads). Circle radius grows with the square root of the residents, from about 5 pixels at 40 residents to at most 14 pixels. Pointing at a circle gives its residents and its distance to the nearest scheduled stop. A note under the switch says how many residents live more than an 800 m walk from any scheduled stop (2,251,110 in Snapshot 2026-10, about 69%) and that circles show blocks with 40 or more residents. The note counts blocks of every size. The circles show only the larger ones. The 3D view has the same switch in its Route tab, under Planning layers, with the same circles and note; there a click on a circle gives what pointing at it gives on the 2D map.

coverage.frequency: 2020 population against the stops of the latest build. Stops are re-read every night.

method: network.js (setGaps) and twin3d.js (setGaps). Both filter the rows of population_blocks.json in your browser: distance above 800 and residents of 40 or more.
how_to_read: Large circles in low-service areas mean many residents far from a scheduled stop.
caveats: Stops from expired timetables still count as stops, so a gap can be larger than shown. Públicos, systems with no published timetable and stops mapped only in OpenStreetMap are not counted, so a gap can also be smaller.
Distances are straight lines and counts are from 2020. It is a planning aid, not a demand forecast.

3D view, Route tab: switch on Residents far from service

source_detail: population_blocks.json, Snapshot 2026-10: 36,570 rows of 2020 Census blocks, each with longitude, latitude, residents and metres to the nearest scheduled stop. The circles carry no credit line of their own.

name: Integration points switch (2D Transit tab and 3D Route tab)
plain: 'Integration points' marks the places where a stop of one transit system lies within 250 metres of a stop of another system. These are natural places to line up timetables, fares and signs.
definition: The switch is off when the page opens. Each point is a white circle with a blue outline, placed midway between the two stops. There are 366 in Snapshot 2026-10, and all are drawn. Pointing at a point names the two operators, the two stops and the distance between them. A note under the switch gives the number found and, when some are left out, says how many are drawn. The 3D view has the same switch in its Route tab, under Planning layers; there a click on a point gives what pointing at it gives on the 2D map.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time.

method: network.js (setXfer) and twin3d.js (setXfer) draw the transfers list of operators.json.
how_to_read: A short distance means two systems have stops at almost the same place.
caveats: A pair shows that stops are close. It does not show that riders can transfer: the observatory does not compare timetables, walking routes or fares.
Stops of expired timetables are included.

view.label: 2D map: Integration points
3D view, Route tab: switch on Integration points
