name: Route planner (2D Transit tab and 3D Route tab)
plain: The route planner draws a route between places you name or click, along roads, and then counts the residents and places it would reach. It is on the Transit tab of the 2D map and on the Route tab of the 3D view.
definition: The planner draws a route between up to eight points and scores it against the open data. Drag a lettered marker to move a point. The route follows roads unless you switch 'Follow roads' off. The card shows the length and an indicative running time, then what the route would reach. The parts are listed below. The chosen points are kept in the page address as r=lat,lng;lat,lng, to 4 decimals (about 11 metres).

coverage.frequency: Computed in your browser each time you plan a route, from the files of the latest build.

method: plan.js is shared by both pages. It matches names against the place-name index (gazetteer.json), routes along the roads with roads.js on roads.bin, and scores the route against the open data. The 2D map draws the route with network.js. The 3D view draws it with twin3d.js. Everything runs in the browser.
how_to_read: Use it to compare options. Read each number on the card with its own entry.
caveats: It is a planning aid. It is not an engineering study or a demand forecast.

The running time uses planning speeds without stops or traffic. When some legs cannot follow roads (for example between islands), the length and the time still include them, as straight lines timed at 8 m/s (28.8 km/h).
The place boxes can offer an online address lookup. That sends the text you typed to OpenStreetMap Nominatim. See the search entry.
The GeoJSON file carries the licenses of its inputs. Check each before you publish it.

The address holds the exact coordinates of every point, to about 11 metres. If a start, end or stop is your home or workplace, anyone with the link can see it. Remove the r= part before you share a link, or use points that are not private.

Tourism places within 400 m of the route are counted only when the tourism place listings are loaded (switch on 'Tourism places' in the Map layers tab, then plan again). Otherwise that tile shows a dash and says so; it is never a zero.
Tourism places are offered as start, stop or end points only once the tourism place listings are loaded; until then the place boxes search the town, street, landmark, stop and route index only.

name: Analysis tab
plain: The Analysis tab puts yearly datasets on the map: jobs, pay, unemployment, income, poverty, commuting, federal money, housing and reported crime. Shade a rate, size a count, move the year, and click the map to see every layer at that place.
definition: In Snapshot 2026-10 the tab lists 549 datasets: 275 yearly series for the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico, and 274 counts and shares for a single year (tourism places, places in a flood hazard area or a protected area, the tourism places near transit, transit stops and the residents near them, whether Uber lists the municipality, the change in median gross rent since 2008-2012, land by plan class, and the residents and housing units inside a hazard, inside protected land or near a stop, the health center sites and shortage areas of each municipality, its hospitals and other care facilities, the distance from where residents live to the nearest health center, its drinking water systems (and those outside PRASA, with the residents they serve) and power plants, its expected yearly loss from natural hazards, the landslides mapped after Hurricane María, its wetlands and mangroves, its public housing developments and units, its tax credit housing projects and units, fire, EMS and police stations and public libraries, its tax-exempt organizations by field, its places on the National Register of Historic Places, its substance use and mental health treatment facilities by type, and its EPA-regulated sites, impaired waters and air quality non-attainment areas, households with severe housing problems, street intersections and drive time to a general hospital, which also have barrio values; and the WCRP vulnerability indices, which have values for barrios only). Of the 275 series, 104 are listed in the economy file (some take their values from the Housing page's series, such as poverty and median income) and 171 more come from the Housing page's series (33), from the Population series of the survey (30), from the daytime population series (3), from the survey's series of labor force participation by sex (7), from the education series of public schools and colleges (7), from the Medicare series (3), from the bridges series (3), from the series of community resilience and earthquakes (5), from the airport and ferry series (4), from the night-time lights series (2), from the satellite fire detections series (3), from the fixed broadband series (6), from the road traffic series (6), from the road deaths series (6), from the bank offices and home loans series (6), from the drought series (3), from the storm recovery series (2), from the essentials series (7), from the degrees series (11), from the school conditions series (4), from the test results series (2), from the health providers series (7) and from the cut-off series (5). Any dataset can be added to the map as a shaded layer or as sized symbols. Up to two shaded layers and any number of symbol layers can be on at once. The tab holds a year control, six ready-made views and the list of layers on the map with their settings. It also has buttons for the workbench, for clearing the layers and for copying a link, switches for other map layers, the dataset list with a search box, four reading notes and a list of sources with their licenses. The tab loads its data the first time you open it. While the tab is open and a layer is visible, a click on the map opens the economy popup, not the municipality profile.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js reads data/economy_series.json (built by economy_series.py) and data/housing_series.json (built by housing_series.py). A housing series that the economy file does not list is added under a 'Housing ·' group. The five tourism counts are built in the browser from municipalities.json.
how_to_read: Start from a ready-made view, then change one thing at a time. Each layer says which year it shows.
caveats: Jobs, pay and establishments count the workplace (Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, QCEW). Income, poverty and commuting describe residents (American Community Survey, ACS). In the 2024 data of Snapshot 2026-10, 9 of the 78 municipalities have more jobs than employed residents; San Juan (1.9 jobs per employed resident) and Mayagüez (1.5) have the most. This fits commuting into job centres, but the ratio does not measure commuting.

Survey figures (ACS, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, LAUS) are noisy for small municipalities. Margins of error are shown where the source publishes them. The jobs data hide cells that would identify one employer, so some sectors are blank in small municipalities.
The informal economy is not in the jobs data. The share of self-employed residents points to some work the jobs data miss, but it is not a measure of the informal economy.

Federal awards are placed where the work is done, as the awarding agency reports it. The awarding agency often records awards for statewide programs under the capital, so San Juan's total can include money that serves other places. See the entry on federal awards, all types.

In Snapshot 2026-10 the latest year (2025) of the jobs and unemployment series is preliminary and can be revised. The unemployment rate has no 2020 value. Some series are not yearly: four census series hold only 2010 and 2020, and the recovery series of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) are by declaration year (12 years from 2001 to 2024 for Public Assistance).
Federal award and recovery amounts (federal awards, FEMA Public Assistance and FEMA Individual Assistance) are amounts obligated (committed) or approved. They are not money spent, damage or need.
Values per resident step in 2020, because the Census Bureau's population estimates change base that year (see the entry on the 2020 break in the population series).

name: Analysis tab: dataset list and search
plain: The dataset list on the Analysis tab shows every dataset in groups. Type in the search box to find one, then press 'Shade' or 'Symbols' to put it on the map, or the info button to read its definition and sources.
definition: In Snapshot 2026-10 the list has 101 groups, shown below with the number of datasets in each. The search box looks for the text you type, as one phrase (not word by word), ignoring accents and capitals, in each dataset's name, group, source reference and definition. A search opens every group that has a match. Without a search only the first group is open. The count beside 'Datasets' shows how many are listed. Each row gives the name and the years it covers (for example 2014–2025, or 'snapshot 2026'), with '± margins' when the source publishes margins of error. 'Shade' adds the dataset as a shaded layer. For a count it is shown per 1,000 residents, and for a dollar total per resident, because a shaded map of a raw count mostly shows how big the municipality is. 'Symbols' adds it as sized circles with the value as published. The info button opens the dataset dialog.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecLoad, ecRenderBrowse). Groups appear in the order of sortGroups in core/datasets.js, the themes of the layer menu (docs/layers.md): population, the economy, hazards and environment, land and housing, infrastructure and mobility, community services, communities, and the visitor economy (Tourism supply) last.
how_to_read: The group is the tab's own grouping. It is not the dictionary's grouping.
caveats: A dataset can appear under a different group here than in the dictionary. For example, poverty, median income and population are listed under groups of the economy file, and housing series appear under 'Housing ·' groups.

name: Analysis tab: shaded layers
plain: A shaded layer colours each municipality by one dataset. The Analysis tab allows two shaded layers at a time. Colours run from light to dark in five groups.
definition: A third shaded layer is refused with a message that says to remove one or to show the new dataset as symbols. Open 'Settings' on a layer's card to change its options. The class limits are set from the values of the 78 municipalities, not from the Puerto Rico figure. With 'Same classes in every year' on, which is the start setting, the limits use the values of all years together, so one colour means the same number in every year. Turn it off to use only the year on screen. The legend lists the range of each class and how many municipalities fall in it. A municipality with no value is grey (#EDEDED), and the legend counts it as 'No data'. The settings are listed below.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecAdd, ecBreaks, ecClass, ecRenderMap, ecRenderLegend). Natural breaks use the Jenks method, which groups values to keep each class as uniform as possible. When more than 1,500 values are pooled, every n-th value is used. The sheet is a copy of the municipality outlines in its own map pane.
how_to_read: With 'Same classes in every year' on (the start setting) a colour is a class among all municipalities in all years pooled, so one year can have uneven group sizes. Read the legend counts for the numbers. On the diverging scale red means below the centre (below Puerto Rico, or below zero change) and blue means above. Neither means better or worse: a red unemployment rate is a lower rate.
caveats: With 'Same classes in every year' on, some colours may not appear in a year whose values cover a narrower range.
Equal intervals can put most municipalities in one class when one or two are very large.
Shading rates and levels suits comparison between places. Shading a raw count mostly shows how big the municipality is.

view.label: 2D map: shaded poverty rate, 2022

values.Show as: Described in the entry on the 'Show as' options.
values.Classes: Quantiles with equal counts, Equal intervals or Natural breaks.
values.Colours: Blue, Green, Gold, Red or Gray. Each ramp has five colours.
values.Opacity: From 20% to 100%. It starts at 85%. The opacity of the first shaded layer sets the opacity of the sheet.
values.Same classes in every year: A checkbox, on at the start.
values.Diverging scale: Options that compare with a centre (index, difference, location quotient and change) use a diverging scale of five classes: dark red, light red, pale grey, light blue and dark blue. The limits are set as shares of the largest distance from the centre: below −50%, −50% to −10%, within ±10%, +10% to +50% and above +50%. Red means below the centre and blue means above. Neither means worse or better.
values.Layer card buttons: Hide, move up or down, open information and remove the layer.

source_detail: economy_series.json and housing_series.json. Each dataset's source reference is in its information window. The map draws no credit line for this layer.

name: Analysis tab: sized symbols
plain: A symbol layer draws a circle on each municipality. The circle's area shows the value, so big circles are big amounts. Symbols suit counts and totals such as jobs or dollars.
definition: Each circle is centred on the municipality's centre. The circle for the largest value has a radius of 30 pixels (20 on a phone). Other radii shrink with the square root of the value, so the area is proportional to the value, down to a minimum of 2.5 pixels. Larger circles are drawn first so small ones stay visible. The largest value is taken over all years when 'Same classes in every year' is on, and over the year on screen otherwise. Colours: Red, Blue, Gold, Green or Charcoal. If a dataset can be negative, for example a change since the base year, increases are blue and decreases red. The legend shows three circles at the largest value, at half of it and at a tenth of it. No circle is drawn for Puerto Rico as a whole or for a municipality with no value. The centre is the area-weighted centre of the municipality's largest part, so islands do not pull the point into the sea.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecRenderMap, ecRenderLegend). Circles are Leaflet circle markers in their own map pane. They do not take clicks.
how_to_read: Compare circle sizes between municipalities in the same layer. Do not compare sizes between two different layers.
caveats: The centre of a long or crescent-shaped municipality can fall away from its towns.
Circles overlap in the San Juan area and may hide each other.

view.label: 2D map: jobs as symbols, 2024

source_detail: economy_series.json and housing_series.json. Each dataset's source reference is in its information window. The map draws no credit line for this layer.

name: Analysis tab: two shaded layers together (bivariate map)
plain: When two shaded layers are on, the map shows both at once with nine colours. Each layer is cut into three classes: low, middle and high.
definition: The first visible shaded layer in the list is the horizontal axis of the legend, which increases to the right. The second is the vertical axis, which increases upward. Each layer is cut into three classes, using the class method set on its card: equal counts (terciles), equal intervals or natural breaks. The nine colours run from light grey (low on both), through teal (high on the first only) and magenta (high on the second only), to dark blue (high on both). The legend shows the three-by-three grid and, for each axis, the layer, its year, and the limits of 'low' and 'high'. The legend title says 'terciles of each' only when both layers use equal-count classes. Otherwise it says 'three classes of each'. A municipality with no value in either layer is grey (#EDEDED). In this mode the diverging scale is not used: every layer is cut into three classes.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecRenderMap, ecRenderLegend, EC_BIV). The colour table is indexed by the class of the second layer and then by the class of the first.
how_to_read: Find the dark cells (both high) and the pale ones (both low). Colours that mix show where the two layers disagree.
caveats: The map shows where two things are high or low together. It does not show that one causes the other.
The three classes are relative to the 78 municipalities (all years pooled when 'Same classes in every year' is on). They are not thresholds of any standard.
The two layers may show different years. The legend names each layer's year, so read it before you compare.

view.label: 2D map: poverty rate and unemployment rate together, 2022

source_detail: economy_series.json and housing_series.json. Each dataset's source reference is in its information window. The map draws no credit line for this layer.

name: Analysis tab: the 'Show as' options
plain: Each layer has a 'Show as' menu. It changes the number behind the colour or circle. Choices include as published, per resident, per km², share, index, change and percentile.
definition: The options depend on the kind of dataset. Counts (people, jobs, places) can be shown as published, per 1,000 residents, per km² and as a share of the Puerto Rico total. The jobs datasets (25 in Snapshot 2026-10) can also be shown as a share of the municipality's jobs and as a location quotient. Dollar totals (wages, federal money, recovery money of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, FEMA) can be shown as published, per resident, per km² and, except for federal loans, as a share of the Puerto Rico total. Everything else (rates, ratios and dollar levels such as median income) can be shown as published, as an index or as a difference from Puerto Rico. Every dataset with more than one year also offers 'change since the base year', and every dataset offers 'percentile among municipalities'. The codes below are the ones written in a shared link.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecNormOptions, ecOut, ecCalc). Land area is the land_km2 field of municipalities.json. Population is the population series. Jobs are the jobs series of the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW).
how_to_read: Choose the option that answers your question. 'Per 1,000 residents' compares places of different size. 'Index' and 'difference' compare with the island.
caveats: 'Per 1,000 residents' divides by residents, not by workers. Jobs are counted at the workplace, so places that draw commuters show high values.
A location quotient above 1 says an industry is concentrated. It does not say the industry is large.

For the five tourism-place counts the Analysis tab divides by the latest population estimate (2025 in Snapshot 2026-10), but the Map layers tab, the Rankings tab and the municipality table divide by the 2020 Census count. The two views can differ (San Juan: 10.4 and 10.0 places per 1,000 residents in Snapshot 2026-10).

view.label: 2D map: tourism jobs as a share of all jobs, 2024

values.value: As published. The dataset's own number in its own unit. Offered for every dataset. The start choice for symbols and for rates, ratios and dollar levels.
values.per1000: Per 1,000 residents. The count divided by the municipality's population, times 1,000, rounded to three decimals. Counts only. The start choice when a count is shaded. Population is the value of the population series for the year shown, or for the latest earlier year, or for its first year when the year shown is earlier. The population series changes basis in 2020 (the 2011-2019 estimates were not revised to the 2020 Census), so in Snapshot 2026-10 the island's population steps up 2.9% from 2019 to 2020 (3.1% for the median municipality), and per-resident values drop by about 3% for that reason alone. Changes that cross 2019 to 2020 include the same jump.
values.perkm2: Per km². The value divided by the municipality's land area in square kilometres. Counts and dollar totals.
values.sharePR: % of the Puerto Rico total. The value divided by the dataset's Puerto Rico figure, times 100. Counts and dollar totals. It is not offered for federal loans. Shares can add up to less than 100% when the island figure holds amounts that belong to no municipality, for example FEMA Public Assistance recorded as statewide, federal awards that name no municipality, or jobs hidden in withheld cells.
values.shareJobs: % of the municipality's jobs. Jobs in an industry divided by all jobs in the same municipality (QCEW), times 100. Only the jobs datasets (25 in Snapshot 2026-10), from 2014.
values.lq: Location quotient (Puerto Rico = 1). The industry's share of the municipality's jobs divided by its share of Puerto Rico's jobs. Above 1 means the industry is more concentrated here than on the island as a whole. Only the jobs datasets. Diverging scale centred on 1.
values.perCapita: $ per resident. The dollar total divided by the municipality's population. Dollar totals only. The start choice when a dollar total is shaded. The same break in the population series in 2020 applies. For FEMA Public Assistance and for federal awards the Puerto Rico per-resident value includes money recorded as statewide or naming no municipality, so it is not comparable with a municipality's value.
values.index: Index (Puerto Rico = 100). The value divided by the Puerto Rico value, times 100. Rates, ratios and dollar levels. Diverging scale centred on 100.
values.diff: Difference from Puerto Rico. The value minus the Puerto Rico value, in the dataset's unit (percentage points for percentages). Rates, ratios and dollar levels. Diverging scale centred on 0.
values.change: Change since the base year. For rates and ratios, the value minus the value in the base year (points for percentages). For counts and dollars, the percent change from the base year, blank where the base value is 0. The base year is chosen in 'Change measured from' (2014 at the start). The dataset's latest year at or before it is used. Blank for years up to the base year. Not offered for the five tourism snapshots. Diverging scale centred on 0. Windows of the American Community Survey (ACS) that overlap share most of their sample, so choose a base year at least five years before the year shown.
values.pctile: Percentile among municipalities. The place of the municipality among the 78 when they are sorted from the lowest value (0) to the highest (100). Municipalities with equal values share the lowest of their places. Puerto Rico as a whole has none.

source_detail: economy_series.json and housing_series.json for the datasets, with land area and the tourism counts from municipalities.json. The map draws no credit line for this layer.

name: Analysis tab: inflation-adjusted dollars
plain: The 'Inflation-adjusted' box on a dollar layer restates every year's dollars in the dollars of the latest index year (2025 in Snapshot 2026-10), so years can be compared. It uses the US consumer price index, because the observatory holds no price index for Puerto Rico.
definition: The box appears on layers whose unit is dollars. It multiplies each year's value by the index of the latest index year (2025) divided by the index of that year. The index is the annual average of the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), US city average (1982-84 = 100), which runs from 172.2 in 2000 to 321.943 in 2025 in Snapshot 2026-10. Years before 2010, such as the 2001 to 2009 declaration years of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) datasets, use the index of their own year. For a year outside 2000–2025 the nearest year is used. The legend and the layer title then say '2025 dollars'. The margin of error shown in the inspector is multiplied the same way. With 'Change since the base year', both ends are adjusted. 'Show as' options that divide dollars, such as per resident, work on the adjusted numbers.

coverage.frequency: One index value per year. The latest year of the index sets the reference year.

method: economy.js (cpiFactor, ecCalc). The index values come from the deflator list in the economy file.
how_to_read: Use it to compare a dollar amount across years. It does not change a single year's map. Example: $1,000 in 2015 becomes about $1,358 in 2025 dollars, because 321.943 divided by 237.017 is 1.358. For another worked example see the entry on the inflation adjustment.
caveats: The US index only approximates the prices Puerto Rico residents pay. The page says so.
The tab's note says American Community Survey (ACS) dollars are already in the final year of each five-year window. The adjustment treats that final year as the year of the value.
Dollar amounts as published (not adjusted) are in the dollars of their own year.

view.label: 2D map: average pay, 2015, in 2025 dollars

source_detail: economy_series.json, deflator list (CPI-U annual averages 2000 to 2025). The map draws no credit line for this layer.

name: Analysis tab: year control, Play and base year
plain: One year control moves every layer on the Analysis tab. Choose 'Latest' or a year (2010 to 2025 in Snapshot 2026-10), step with the arrows, drag the slider or press Play to watch the years go by.
definition: In Snapshot 2026-10 the year list has 'Latest' and then 2025 down to 2010. 'Latest' shows each dataset's own last year. A chosen year is used by every layer. A dataset with no value for that year shows its latest earlier year, and the layer says '2022 (latest at or before 2023)'. If the year is earlier than the dataset starts, the layer shows its first year and says 'first data 2014'. Snapshot datasets always say 'snapshot 2026'. Play starts at 2010 (or at the chosen year) and moves one year every 1.4 seconds up to the last year (2025), then stops. Choosing a year by hand stops Play. 'Change measured from' lists every year before the last one (2010 to 2024 in Snapshot 2026-10) and starts at 2014. It sets the base of the 'change since the base year' option only. The year and the base are kept in a shared link (ey and eb).

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecInitYear, ecResolve, ecChip). The years offered are all years from 2010 on that any yearly dataset holds.
how_to_read: Check each layer's year chip before comparing two layers. Layers can show different years under one control.
caveats: In Snapshot 2026-10, 'Latest' and '2025' are not the same: survey datasets end in 2024, so choosing 2025 shows their 2024 value with a note.
American Community Survey (ACS) years are five-year windows labelled by their last year, so neighbouring years share most of their sample. Compare windows that do not overlap for real change.

On Latest, a pair of layers can come from different years (in Snapshot 2026-10, jobs 2025 and ACS 2024). Check each year chip before you compare two layers, read them as a pair or correlate them. In Snapshot 2026-10 the unemployment rate has no 2020 value, so choosing 2020 shows 2019.

view.label: 2D map: unemployment rate in 2020

name: Analysis tab: ready-made views
plain: 'Start from a view' offers six ready-made combinations of layers. One click replaces the layers on the map with that set and shows a short message.
definition: The six views are listed below with the layers each sets. A view replaces all economy layers with its own, each at its start settings (classes of equal counts, 'Same classes in every year' on). It also sets the other map layers, so that the view is not buried under pins. It keeps on only the layer it names (tourism places or transit routes). It turns off tourism places, transit routes, transit stops, barrios, flood zones, protected areas and land use otherwise. The municipality outlines stay as they are. The year and the base year do not change.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecRenderPresets, ecSetContext).
how_to_read: Use a view as a starting point, then open each layer's settings to adjust it.
caveats: A view is a combination of layers. It is not a finding.
The Public money view shows federal amounts obligated (committed). They are not money paid, damage or need. See the codes below.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab, 'Poverty and unemployment' set by hand

values.Jobs and pay: Shaded: average pay (qcew_avg_pay). Symbols: jobs (qcew_jobs). No extra layers.
values.Poverty and unemployment: Two shaded layers, so a bivariate map: poverty rate (poverty_pct) and unemployment rate (laus_unemp_rate). Symbols: unemployed residents (laus_unemployed).
values.Job centres and commuting: Two shaded layers, so a bivariate map: jobs per employed resident (jobs_per_employed_resident) and commuters with 45 minutes or more (commute_45plus_pct). Symbols: jobs (qcew_jobs). Also shows transit routes.
values.Public money: Shaded: federal awards per resident (fed_awards_total, 'perCapita'). Symbols: Public Assistance of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), amounts obligated (fema_pa_obligated). These are federal amounts obligated (committed). They are not money paid, not damage and not need. In the 2026-10 snapshot, over all years combined, 77.9% of FEMA Public Assistance money is recorded as statewide and is not in the municipality values (80.9% for the 2017 declarations, 13.1% for 2024, the year this view shows on Latest). Awards that serve the whole island are often booked to the capital.
values.Government and self-employment: Two shaded layers, so a bivariate map: government jobs as a share of all jobs (gov_job_share_pct) and self-employed workers (self_employed_pct).
values.Tourism economy: Shaded: tourism jobs as a share of the municipality's jobs (tourism_jobs, 'shareJobs'). Symbols: accommodation jobs (accommodation_jobs). Also shows the tourism places pins.

name: Analysis tab: 'Also show on the map'
plain: 'Also show on the map' repeats eight switches of the Map layers tab, in the order of that tab and with its names, so you can add context to an economy view without leaving the tab.
definition: The eight switches are Tourism places, Transit routes, Transit stops, Barrios, Flood hazard zones, Protected areas, Land use (PUT 2015, the Plan de Uso de Terrenos) and Municipality boundaries. Each one is the same switch as on the Map layers tab. A change in one place shows in the other.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. Transit data are refreshed every night.

method: economy.js (ecRenderContext, ecContextSync) sets the Layers-tab checkbox and sends it a change event.
how_to_read: Add one context layer at a time. Several overlays together make the economy colours hard to read.
caveats: The sea level and transit planning layers are not in this list. Use the Layers and Transit tabs for them.

view.label: 2D map, Analysis tab: poverty rate in 2022 with flood zones on

name: Analysis tab: click, hover and the municipality card
plain: Click a municipality while the Analysis tab is open. A card shows the value of each visible layer for that place and its rank among the 78. It also shows the margin of error where the source publishes one.
definition: A click outlines the municipality in black and opens a card. The card has a table with one row for each visible layer. A row gives the name (press it to open the dataset's information), how the layer is shown and for which year, and the value. It adds the margin of error (±) when the source publishes one and the layer is shown 'as published'. For a rate the margin is in percentage points (for example ±1.2 pts). For other datasets it is in the dataset's own unit. It ends with the rank ('#n of N', where 1 is the highest value). A link opens the workbench. On a computer, pointing at the map also shows a small box at the bottom right with each layer's value for the municipality under the pointer. That box is not shown on phones. In the workbench's Inspector tab the same table adds a column for Puerto Rico and a column headed 'Trend' with a trend line for each layer. A caption under each line gives its length, for example '12 yrs · 2014–25' (see the entry on trend lines). The map popup has no trend column. When the jobs data are available, a line names the industry sector, or government, that has the most jobs in the municipality, with its share of the municipality's jobs, for the year the jobs dataset shows.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecInspect, ecValue, ecRank, ecHover, ecSelect).
how_to_read: Use the rank to place the municipality, and the margin of error to judge whether a small difference means anything.
caveats: Margins of error are 90% confidence margins from the Census Bureau's survey. Many datasets are counts or administrative figures with no margin.
The rank counts the municipalities that have a value. Tied values share the first of their places.
The 'largest sector' line counts private industry sectors and government. Hidden cells can change it in small municipalities.
Rank 1 is the highest value, which for unemployment or poverty is the worst result. Compare ranks only within the same layer and year.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab, jobs as symbols (click a municipality)

name: Trend lines (sparklines) and their length label
plain: A small grey line with a blue dot shows how a value changed over the years for one municipality. The label under it says how many years the line covers, for example '12 yrs'.
definition: The blue dot marks the year on screen. The label under the line gives the length of the trend: 'N yrs' ('yrs' means years) is the number of calendar years from the first to the last year drawn, both included. If some years have no value, the label adds how many values were drawn, for example '12 yrs, 9 values'. On the Analysis tab the label also gives the first and last year, for example '12 yrs · 2014–25'. The column header of the lines in the workbench's Inspector tab (the map popup has no trend lines) reads 'Trend', with the note 'years shown; dot = chosen year'. The label itself starts with the number of years. The Housing profile has no header. A line needs at least two yearly values, so datasets with one year have none. The line scales from the lowest to the highest value drawn, so a flat-looking line can hold a large change. Economy lines start in 2010 at the earliest. Housing profile lines use every year the dataset has.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecSpark) and housing.js (spark) draw the same small chart. The label is calculated from the years of the values drawn.
how_to_read: Compare the shape and the length, not the height. Two lines of different datasets are each drawn to fill the same small space.
caveats: Survey series (American Community Survey, ACS) use overlapping five-year windows, so their lines are smoother than the real change.
A series with a break, such as the population series that steps up in 2020, shows the break as a jump.
For survey series the length counts window labels. Each label is a five-year window, so the line covers more time than the label says.
The Economy line follows the layer's 'Show as' and inflation settings. The Housing line shows values as published.

view.label: Housing page: municipality profile with trend lines

source_detail: economy_series.json and housing_series.json (the series drawn). The small chart carries no credit line.

name: Economy workbench: panel and Inspector tab
plain: The Workbench is a panel at the bottom of the screen that opens from the Analysis tab. It has ten tabs: Inspector, Table, Scatter, Trend, Correlations, Small multiples, Compare two maps, Composite, Scenarios and Study areas. All of them follow the layers, the year and the settings on the map.
definition: The 'Workbench' button opens the panel beside the side panel, and the button or the × closes it. The panel's header shows the year, or 'Latest year'. Inspector tab: pick a place from the menu, Puerto Rico as a whole included, or click the map. The table gives each visible layer's value for the place, the Puerto Rico value and a trend line with its length under it (see the entry on trend lines). The other tabs are described in their own entries. It also opens from the link 'Open in the workbench' on a municipality card, from 'View the map as a table' at the foot of the map's legend (the Table tab, so every map can be read as a table) and from buttons in the chat.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecBenchOpen, ecRenderBench, ecBenchInspect; the views of plan item 12: ecBenchMatrix, ecBenchMultiples, ecBenchSwipe, ecBenchComposite; docs/workbench.md).
how_to_read: Use the Inspector to answer 'what do all my layers say about this place?'.
caveats: A layer that is hidden (eye closed) does not appear in the workbench.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab (press Workbench)

name: Economy workbench: Table tab
plain: The Table tab lists the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico with one column for each visible layer. Sort by any column, find a municipality by name and download the table as a comma-separated values (CSV) file.
definition: Puerto Rico is the first row. Municipalities follow in alphabetical order, in Spanish collation, until you sort by a column. A click on a column title sorts by it, and a second click reverses the order. A box finds municipalities by name. Each column title gives the dataset, its year and, when it is not 'as published', how it is shown. Values are shown rounded as the layer shows them. The button 'Download CSV' saves pr_economy_layers.csv. Its columns are GEOID (the geographic identifier code of the Census Bureau), Municipality and one column for each visible layer, named '<dataset> (<year note>; <show-as code>)'. The file has 79 rows, the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico, in the order of the data file whatever the sort on screen. Values in the file are not rounded for display.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecBenchTable, ecSaveCsv).
how_to_read: Use the table to look up exact values. Use the CSV to analyse them.
caveats: The CSV holds the values as currently shown, after any 'Show as' option or inflation adjustment. The file does not repeat the margins of error.
Download all years of one dataset, with margins, from its information dialog.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab (press Workbench, then Table)

name: Economy workbench: Scatter tab
plain: The Scatter tab plots one visible layer against another, one dot for each municipality, and gives the correlation between them. It needs two visible layers.
definition: Pick the X and Y layers. Each dot is a municipality, and a click on a dot selects it on the map. 'Log scales' draws both axes on a logarithmic scale and keeps only dots where both values are above zero. 'Size by population' scales each dot by the population of the X layer's year. The note above the chart gives the number of municipalities and the correlation coefficient r. A dashed line shows the straight line of best fit (least squares), drawn only when log scales are off. Axis limits are set from the data with a small margin.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecBenchScatter). r is the Pearson correlation of the plotted values. It is calculated on the values themselves, not on their logarithms, even when log scales are on. The chart is drawn with Chart.js.
how_to_read: r runs from −1 to 1. Near 0 means little straight-line relationship. Near ±1 means the dots follow a line closely. The two layers can show different years, so check the chips in the axis titles. With log scales on, the dots look straighter but r still measures the straight-line fit of the raw values, and the fitted line is hidden.
caveats: A correlation across places is not cause and effect. Large places, small samples and survey noise can drive it.
The page says this in the note above the chart.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab (press Workbench, then Scatter)

name: Economy workbench: Trend tab
plain: The Trend tab draws one line for each chosen place over the years, for one visible layer. Add places, hide lines by clicking their names, and compare each place with Puerto Rico.
definition: Pick a layer (datasets with only one year are not listed) and add places from the menu. The lines follow the layer's settings, such as per 1,000 residents or change since the base year. Years run from 2010 (datasets of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, FEMA, also show earlier years). The Puerto Rico line is thicker. A click on a name in the legend hides or shows that line. 'Reset places' keeps Puerto Rico and the selected municipality. Clicking municipalities on the map adds them. The chart shows up to eight places.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecBenchTrend). Places are kept as a set. The chart draws up to eight of them: Puerto Rico first, then the municipalities in the order of the municipality list. Puerto Rico is never the one left out.
how_to_read: Compare slopes between places. Check the unit on the vertical axis.
caveats: With more than eight places chosen, the municipalities that come last in the list drop out of the chart without a message. Puerto Rico always stays.

The horizontal axis lists only the years the dataset holds, evenly spaced. In Snapshot 2026-10, a missing year (the unemployment rate has no 2020) or uneven years (FEMA Public Assistance holds 12 declaration years from 2001 to 2024) do not show as gaps, so time can look compressed. The vertical axis is fitted to the data and need not start at zero, so slopes look steeper than the percentage change. A municipality with no value in a listed year is bridged by a straight line.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab (press Workbench, then Trend)

name: Analysis tab: dataset information window
plain: The info button beside a dataset opens a window with its definition, years, sources and licenses. It also links to the dataset's dictionary entry and lets you download all its years as a comma-separated values (CSV) file.
definition: The window shows the dataset's group and type (count, dollar total, dollar level, rate or ratio) and a definition. Jobs (qcew_jobs) and the unemployment rate (laus_unemp_rate) have an extra note. Next come the source reference and the years the dataset covers (for example '2014–2025 (12 years)', with 'margins of error at 90% confidence are published' when they are). Then come the geography, the build date and a note on dollars where they apply. A line 'Full entry' links to the dataset's entry in the data dictionary, where you find its meaning, method, cautions and how to cite it. For Public Assistance of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) the window also gives the share of money recorded as statewide for each declaration year. For the federal award datasets it gives the share of awards that name no municipality, by fiscal year. Below are the sources with their license text and links. Buttons add the dataset to the map as a shaded layer or as symbols. 'Download all years (CSV)' saves pr_economy_<dataset>.csv with the columns GEOID (the geographic identifier code), Municipality and one column for each year, plus a margin-of-error column for each year when the source publishes one. Values are as published. Nothing is normalised or inflation-adjusted.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year control runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: economy.js (ecInfo), which fills an HTML dialog element. The dictionary link opens dictionary.html#economy.<dataset>, or #housing.<dataset> for series that come from the Housing page.
how_to_read: Read the definition and the source before you cite a number. The dictionary entry gives the full method and a citation.
caveats: The license text is what the source states. Check the source's own terms before you reuse the data.
The CSV can start earlier than 2010 because it holds every year of the dataset.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab, dataset list

name: Ask the observatory (chat)
plain: 'Ask the observatory' is a chat box that answers questions about the Analysis tab's datasets, in English or Spanish. It is not a language model. Every answer is built from numbers computed in your browser, and nothing you type leaves your browser unless you choose to open the GitHub request form.
definition: 'Ask the observatory' answers questions about the datasets of the Analysis tab (549 in Snapshot 2026-10) and the map layers, in English or Spanish. Type up to 400 characters. Each answer is in the language of the question. A reply can hold text, small tables, links and buttons. It can also change the map: shade datasets, switch on layers, set the year, select a municipality, move the map to a place, shade the barrios of a municipality or open the workbench. When the observatory has no data for what you ask, the answer shows the nearest dataset and says that it is an approximation and what is missing. A question the chat cannot match, or answers only with an approximation, is saved on your device in a wishlist without asking, so do not type personal information. The codes below describe how to open it, what it remembers and what it can and cannot answer.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the page is updated.

method: chat.js and ask.js. 1. The question is cleaned: accents and capitals are removed. In a short question, a word one letter from a topic of the observatory is read as that topic (two letters from eight letters on), and the answer says so. 2. Municipality names are found, and some well-known place names (Santurce, Isla Verde, Levittown) with their municipality. 3. chat.js's word list turns words into dataset keys, from specific phrases to general ones. 4. ask.js (loaded with the first question) reads the question again with a lexicon of everyday words in both languages, Puerto Rican ones included (guagua, carro público, la AMA, la AAA, la luz, cuido, chavos, derrumbes, envejecientes), the names of the map layers, the glossary terms and the words of the datasets' own names. It finds the topics that step 3 left, the layers, a time ("después de María" is 2017) and what must not be drawn. 5. Two topics are composed: a topic that a map layer shows (transit) turns that layer on, the other is shaded, and the answer gives the correlation of the two across municipalities. 6. Rules choose the kind of answer (see the entry on answer types). 7. A handler computes the answer from the Analysis tab's dataset values and writes the sentences from templates, with the source, period and geography of what it shows. No server is called. No language model is used.
how_to_read: Ask short questions that name a dataset: 'unemployment', 'rent', 'tourism jobs'. Add a municipality or a year to narrow the answer.
caveats: The chat matches words. An unusual phrasing can still fail, and a word can match a dataset by chance: the word 'bar', for example, selects restaurant and bar jobs.
Answers find patterns across places. They do not show causes.
An approximation is not the measure you asked for: the answer names what is missing (for example, there are no traffic data, so commutes of 45 minutes or more stand in).
Transit layers and vehicles follow scheduled timetables (GTFS), not live positions.

An answer that puts datasets on the map replaces the layers on the Analysis tab. It also switches off tourism places, transit routes, barrios, flood zones, protected areas and land use, unless the question names them. A question that names only layers adds them and leaves the rest as it is.
Sensitive places are counted, never drawn: the chat never shows shelters for victims of violence, a person's home or contact details, or health facilities as points.
When the chat saves a question, its reply says it added the request 'so the team can see what people ask for'. The request stays on your device unless you copy it or open the GitHub form.

view.label: 2D map: press 'Ask' in the top bar

values.Opening it: Press the 'Ask' button in the top bar of the 2D map, or a suggested question in the About tab. The window's language follows your browser at first and changes with the 'ES' or 'EN' button. The bin button clears the conversation.
values.Memory: The chat remembers the datasets, year and municipality of the last answer, so a follow-up such as 'Where is it highest?' works.
values.What it can answer: The datasets of the Analysis tab (549 in Snapshot 2026-10), found by their rules, by their own names in English and Spanish, by the words their dictionary entry lists for asking, or by everyday words (vivienda, transporte, guaguas, la luz). Two topics at once ('transporte y vivienda': the routes and stops, with rent shaded). A layer by its name or an everyday name ('rutas de guagua', 'zonas inundables', 'bomberos'), on the 2D map and the 3D view; on the 3D view also the terrain, the 3D buildings, the scheduled vehicles, the storm tracks and the routes by trips in the hour. A place and a topic ('pobreza en Santurce'); the barrios of a municipality ranked ('¿qué barrios de Ponce tienen más pobreza?') for datasets with barrio values; a municipality's own change in a trend. Two places or more side by side, a place's profile, a composite index. The definition of a glossary term ('¿qué es el margen de error?') and the source of a layer. 'What data is missing?' from the wanted-data list and 'How big is the database?' from the data inventory.
values.What it cannot answer: Questions about single tourism places, live transit positions, or topics the observatory has no data for (traffic, outages, diseases): for these it shows the nearest dataset, says it is an approximation and adds the question to the wishlist.

name: Ask the observatory: the kinds of answer
plain: The chat gives one of about twenty kinds of answer, chosen by rules from the words in your question. This entry lists them with an example of each.
definition: The rules look first for what must not be drawn (a shelter for victims of violence, a person's home, drug points) and for a term to define, then for clear words (clear, missing, patterns, size, help, sources, catalog), unless such a word is part of a topic ('agua limpia', 'ayuda federal'), then for two or more datasets with comparing words, then for trend words, then for ranking words. A municipality name alone gives its profile. One dataset with a municipality gives that municipality's value. Datasets without other words are shown on the map; layers without datasets are switched on. A bare year changes the year. Anything else falls to the last answer, which suggests datasets.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the page is updated.

method: chat.js (chIntent, chRefine and the Handlers) and ask.js. The answers use the same functions as the Analysis tab: values, ranks and the correlation.
how_to_read: If an answer is not what you wanted, name the dataset more directly or open the Analysis tab.
caveats: A question can match more than one kind. The rules pick the first that fits, in the order given above.
The 'missing' list names candidate datasets that are not in the observatory. The source, license and terms of a candidate are not yet confirmed.

view.label: 2D map: press 'Ask' and try 'Where is unemployment highest?'

values.show: Name one to four datasets without comparing words, for example 'Show poverty and rent'. The chat puts them on the map (rates as shading, counts as sized symbols), then says where the first one is highest and lowest and what the Puerto Rico figure is. With two datasets it adds the correlation when it is 0.3 or stronger. A year in the question sets the year.
values.value: A dataset and a municipality, for example 'Unemployment in Ponce': the municipality's value, its place among the 78 (highest first) and the Puerto Rico value. For counts it also gives the per-resident view.
values.rank: Words such as highest, lowest, top, best, worst or 'where is': a table of the top municipalities and the Puerto Rico value. The table has 5 rows at the start. A number in the question ('top 10') sets the length, up to 15. For counts a second table gives the per-resident ranking. Words such as lowest, least, bottom or fewest turn the table around. The words best and worst do not change the order. Both return the highest values, so 'where is unemployment best?' returns the highest unemployment rates. Use lowest or least for the other end. With one municipality named ('¿dónde en Bayamón es más alto el alquiler?'), the table ranks its barrios when the dataset has barrio values, and the map is shaded by barrio; otherwise the answer gives the municipality's place among the 78 first.
values.compare: Two or more datasets with words such as related, versus, together or compare, for example 'Show poverty and unemployment together' or 'poverty vs rent': the correlation of the first two across municipalities, the biggest exceptions and a scatter plot.
values.trend: One dataset with words such as changed, since, trend or over time: Puerto Rico's change between the first and last year (or the years you name) and the three municipalities that rose most and fell most. Municipalities that start with a count below 50 or a dollar total below $100,000 are not ranked in these two lists. The numbers in the text use the dollars of each year, but for dollar datasets the map the chat opens is inflation-adjusted, so its colours and the sentences can disagree. If no municipality fell, the second list is headed 'Rose least'. The map shows the change since the first year and the trend chart opens. With one municipality named, the answer gives that municipality's change first and its place among the 78 by change, and selects it on the map.
values.municipality: A municipality name alone: a table of 12 indicators (population, poverty, median household income, unemployment rate, jobs, average pay, jobs per employed resident, government job share, tourism jobs share, long commutes, median rent and federal awards per resident) with its value, the Puerto Rico value and its place among the 78, and a line naming the ones where it is in the top or bottom five.
values.sources: Words such as sources, license, definition, 'what does X mean' or 'how is X measured' with one to three datasets: the definition, the years, source links with licenses, a button 'Open the full source details' for each dataset and a button 'Entry in the data dictionary' (in Spanish 'Entrada en el diccionario de datos') that opens the dictionary entry of the first dataset.
values.catalog: 'What data do you have?': the dataset groups with their counts, or the datasets on a topic you name (up to 14 listed). Buttons offer 'See everything that is missing' and 'Open the data dictionary'.
values.insights: Words such as patterns, interesting or surprising: where jobs concentrate, and up to five of the strongest links between datasets from different areas of life. Each can be shown on the map. The line about jobs and residents compares workplace jobs with residents. It can reflect employers that report all workers at one site as well as commuting. It is a lead, not a measure of commuting.
values.missing: 'What data is missing?' or 'wish list': the candidate datasets of the wanted-data list (30 in Snapshot 2026-10), grouped by theme, with status, update frequency and license, and the requests kept on your device.
values.size: 'How big is the database?': the size of the published data and the five biggest files.
values.year: A bare year such as '2019' sets the year control.
values.clear: 'Clear' or 'reset' empties the Analysis tab's layers and the selected municipality. Other map layers stay as they are.
values.help: 'Help' or a greeting: a short description and example questions.
values.fallback: Anything else: 'I could not match that to a dataset', the closest datasets by word overlap and any matching entries of the wanted-data list. A question with two or more content words is also added to the wishlist on your device.
values.layers: A layer named alone, for example 'Muestra las rutas de guagua' or 'zonas inundables en Toa Baja': the layer is switched on (it shows in the 'layers on' chip, and 'Turn all off' and Undo treat it like any other), the map moves to the place if one is named, and the answer says where the layer comes from and offers the datasets that go with it.
values.explain: 'What is X?' or 'qué significa X' for a glossary term: its definition and source, with a link to the glossary. For a layer: where it comes from.
values.sensitive: A question about a shelter for victims of violence, a person's home or contact details, or drug points: the answer says that the observatory never shows them, and draws nothing; for drug points it shows the reported crimes of the municipality.
values.nodata: A topic the observatory has nothing on (elections, places of worship, shelters): the answer says so, adds the question to the wishlist and offers the nearest layers as buttons.
values.crisis: A question about suicide, self-harm or overdose deaths: the answer says that the observatory has no data on this and gives the 988 line and, in Puerto Rico, the Línea PAS of ASSMCA (Administración de Servicios de Salud Mental y Contra la Adicción): 1-800-981-0023, 24 hours, free and confidential, or its chat at lineapas.assmca.pr.gov. Nothing is shaded, no place is ranked and the question is not a data wish. The treatment answer to 'near me' gives findtreatment.gov (SAMHSA) and the same two lines. Both answers end with the sources of that sentence, linked: ASSMCA's home page (https://assmca.pr.gov/), which states every fact of it (the number, 24 hours, free, confidential and the chat), and the Línea PAS site (https://lineapas.assmca.pr.gov/), which states the number, 24 hours and the chat; checked 2026-10-21. The glossary term Línea PAS cites ASSMCA's Línea PAS page (https://assmca.pr.gov/linea-pas).

name: Ask the observatory: what stays on your device
plain: The chat runs in your browser. What you type is not sent to Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) or to any other server, unless you press the button that opens the GitHub request form. Two small items are kept on your device: your language choice and a wishlist of questions the chat could not answer.
definition: The chat reads the observatory's own data files and makes no other call. It keeps one item in your browser's storage: a wishlist (twin.wishlist.v1) of up to 50 questions it could not answer, each with the date. The language you chose is kept by the page, not by the chat (twin.lang, in local storage and, for the current visit, in session storage). You can see the wishlist in the answer to 'What data is missing?'. The conversation itself is not stored. It is gone when you close or reload the page. The one place where text you type leaves the page is the online address lookup of the search box. It is not part of the chat. The codes below describe the two buttons that sit under the wishlist.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the page is updated.

method: chat.js (chAddWish, chCopyWish, chIssueUrl). The issue address is https://github.com/Foundation-for-Puerto-Rico/pr-data-observatory/issues/new with the title and body in the address, so you can read the text before you submit.
how_to_read: Do not type personal information into the chat. It is not needed, and it would be kept in your wishlist if the chat could not answer.
caveats: Clearing the site data in your browser removes the wishlist.
Page loads still send the usual requests (the page's own files, fonts, libraries and map tiles) to other servers, which can see your IP address.
The GitHub button sends the wishlist text to GitHub when the new tab opens, before you submit the form. See the codes below.

The 'See in 3D' button opens the 3D view with your question in the address after the '#' sign. That part of an address is not sent to any server, but it stays in the browser's history, and in the link if you copy it.

view.label: 2D map: press 'Ask'

values.Copy button: Copies the wishlist text so that you can paste it where you choose.
values.GitHub button: Opens GitHub in a new tab with your unanswered questions already in the web address, so GitHub receives that text when the tab opens, before you submit anything. No issue exists until you submit the form. An issue you submit on GitHub can be seen by others, depending on the repository's settings. Remove any personal information from the list before you press the button.

name: Ask the observatory: correlations and patterns
plain: When you ask how two datasets relate, the chat measures how closely they move together across the municipalities. The number is called r and runs from −1 to 1. If the link is not weak, the chat names the biggest exceptions.
definition: r is the Pearson correlation of the two datasets across the municipalities that have both values, and it needs at least 8. Each dataset is used in its default form: per 1,000 residents for counts, per resident for dollar totals and as published for the rest, in the latest year or the year you name. If the absolute value of r is below 0.3 the chat says the datasets 'show little relationship'. Above that it says they 'rise together' (r above 0) or 'move in opposite directions' (r below 0). When the absolute value of r is 0.3 or more, the answer also names up to three exceptions: the municipalities farthest from the line of best fit, which is the straight line that runs closest to all the dots. The 'patterns' answer is described below.

coverage.frequency: Calculated each time you ask, from the data of the latest build.

method: chat.js (chPearson, chInsights, Tools.correlate). The scatter chart of the workbench uses the same coefficient.
how_to_read: r is the Pearson correlation. 0 means no straight-line link between the two. 1 means the places line up perfectly. −1 means they line up in opposite directions. A strong r says the two move together across places.
caveats: A pattern across places is not proof that one thing causes the other. Large places, small samples and survey noise can drive it. The chat says this in its answer.
The rules about which pairs count as expected are a choice made in the code. They are not statistical tests.

The chat screens many pairs and shows the strongest, so some links arise by chance. Federal award and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance figures per resident are among the 26 datasets, even though part of that money cannot be placed in a municipality and awards for the whole island are often booked to the capital. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the share of federal award dollars that name no municipality runs from 3.4% to 24.7% by fiscal year, and the share of Public Assistance recorded as statewide runs from 11.0% to 88.3% by declaration year. A link that involves them may reflect where money is booked, not need. When you do not name a year, each dataset uses its own latest year. Treat every result as a question to check, not a finding.

view.label: 2D map: press 'Ask' and try 'What are the most interesting patterns?'

values.Patterns (the 'patterns' answer): The chat compares pairs of 26 datasets from different areas of life and lists at most five. The pairs, cut-offs and results are in the entry on the patterns ranking.

source_detail: economy_series.json and housing_series.json, read in your browser. The chat draws no credit line. Its 'sources' answer gives the source links.

name: Search box (2D map, 3D view and route planner)
plain: The search box at the top finds municipalities, barrios, towns, streets, Puerto Rico (PR) highway numbers, landmarks, transit stops and routes, and tourism places. What you type is matched in your browser, except when you choose the online address lookup.
definition: Press / to jump to the box. Results start after 2 characters, and up to 12 are listed, each with an icon, a label and a line of detail. The arrow keys move through the list, Enter picks the first or the focused result, and Escape closes it. Two decimal numbers such as 18.4655, -66.1057 are read as coordinates. After 4 characters the list ends with 'Look up ... as an address online'. A pick flies the map there and drops a pin whose popup has 'Route from here' and 'Route to here'. What the box searches and what a pick does are listed below.

coverage.frequency: The place-name index is rebuilt with each full build. Stops and routes are re-read every night.

method: plan.js (parseQuery, textScore, Gaz, attachSearch, searchEverything), shared by the 2D and 3D pages. Names are compared without accents or capitals. The online lookup asks nominatim.openstreetmap.org for up to 6 results inside a box around Puerto Rico (countrycodes=pr, bounded) and shows the first two parts of each address.
how_to_read: Type part of a name. If a street has several matches, add the municipality.
caveats: The online address lookup sends the text you typed to OpenStreetMap's Nominatim service, which has its own usage policy. It runs only when you pick that line. Nothing else you type leaves the page.
A misspelling finds nothing. Matching is on letters, after accents and capitals are removed.

The 2D tourism results follow your category, confidence and worship filters, so a place can be missing because a filter hides it. They appear only once the tourism place listings are loaded: until then the last line of the results offers to load them (about 3.0 MB compressed in Snapshot 2026-10).

view.label: 2D map: search box
3D view: search box

values.Places and areas: Municipalities and the place-name index. The index holds towns, communities, barrios, neighbourhoods, PR highways, named streets, hospitals, schools, colleges, public buildings, terminals, parks, beaches, mountains, water, landmarks, airports and shopping centres.
values.Tourism places: Searched by name or type. On the 2D map the box follows the current category, confidence and worship filters. In the 3D view it follows the category buttons, confidence 0.50 and no places of worship.
values.Transit: Scheduled stops, stations, terminals and airports by name. The header box also searches transit routes by number, name or operator. The planner's boxes search the same list without routes.
values.A pick on the 2D map: A municipality opens its profile, a tourism place opens its card, a stop opens its card and a route fits on the screen.
values.A pick in the 3D view: The camera flies to the result, or fits the municipality or route, and a pin card opens.

name: Shareable link of the 2D map
plain: The 2D map keeps its view in the part of the page address after the # sign: municipality, position, layers that are on, shading, planned route and economy layers. Copy the address to share the view.
definition: The address is rewritten about a quarter of a second after each change, without adding steps to the browser's back button. Its form is #<Municipality>&c=<lat>,<lng>,<zoom>&l=<layers>&s=<shading>&r=<route>&e=<economy>&ey=<year>&eb=<base>&slr=<feet>. Parts that do not apply are left out, except c and l, which are always written. The parts are listed below. When the address changes while the page is open, the municipality, position, layers, shading and sea level are applied again. The route (r) and the economy parts (e, ey, eb) are read only when the page loads. To use a changed one, reload the page. The page's title carries the municipality name. The '3D + Time' link in the header carries the position (c) and the route (r) to the 3D view.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the page is updated.

method: app.js (writeHash, parseHash, applyHash, LAYER_KEYS), network.js and economy.js.
how_to_read: Open the link in a new tab to check it before you share it. A hand-made link must list every layer you want on. Example: index.html#c=18.4400,-66.0900,12&l=muni,flood&s=sfha_pct shows the flood zones and shades the municipalities by the share of places in a flood hazard area, with no pins.
caveats: Layer settings other than those listed, such as the category buttons, the confidence slider, the worship switch and the open tab, are not kept in the address.
A link records choices, not data. If the observatory's data change after a new snapshot, the same link can show different numbers.

The r= part holds the exact coordinates of every point of a planned route, to about 11 metres. If a start, end or stop is your home or workplace, anyone with the link can see it. Remove the r= part before you share a link, or use points that are not private.

view.label: 2D map: flood zones, shaded by flood exposure
2D map: a municipality

values.#<Municipality>: A municipality name, URL-encoded, such as #San%20Juan. It is matched ignoring accents and capitals. An unknown name gives a message. A link with a municipality opens the Municipality tab.
values.c: c=<latitude>,<longitude>,<zoom>: the map centre (4 decimals) and the zoom level, a whole number on the 2D map's scale. When c is present the map does not fly to the municipality.
values.l: l=<layers>: the layers that are ON, separated by commas. The list is complete: a layer that is not named is switched off, including tourism places (places) and boundaries (muni). A link with l=flood therefore shows no pins and no boundaries.
values.l=taxi: Taxi stands and electric vehicle charging.
values.s: s=<field>: a measure of the retired 'Shade municipalities by' menu, for example s=sfha_pct. Old links keep working: the measure opens as its dataset (app.js SHADE_DS) and the address is rewritten with e=.
values.slr: slr=<feet>: the sea level slider, a whole number from 1 to 10. It is written only when the sea level layer is on.
values.r: r=<lat>,<lng>;<lat>,<lng>...: the points of a planned route, 4 decimals, from 2 to 8 points. The link opens the Transit tab and plans the route.
values.e, ey, eb: The Analysis tab's layers, year and base year. See the entry on Economy links.

name: Shareable link of the Analysis tab
plain: The Analysis tab writes its layers, year and base year into the page address. The 'Copy link' button copies the address, and opening it brings the same layers back.
definition: The part e= holds the layers, in list order, separated by commas (written %2C in the address). Each layer is ten items joined by dots: <dataset>.<mode>.<show-as>.<ramp>.<classes>.<visible>.<fixed>.<inflation>.<opacity>.<colour>. For example poverty_pct.f.value.blue.q.1.1.0.85.0 is a shaded poverty rate, as published, in blue, with equal-count classes, visible, the same classes in every year, not inflation-adjusted, at 85% opacity. A link with an e= part opens the Analysis tab. These parts are read only when the page loads. If you change them in a page that is already open, reload it. To keep other map layers out of the way, add l=muni (see the 2D link entry). The first two shaded layers form the bivariate map.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the page is updated.

method: economy.js (ecEncode, ecRestore, ECON.extra). The button 'Copy link' (ecCopy) writes the address and copies it. If your browser blocks the copy, a message asks you to copy the address from the address bar.
how_to_read: Build a link by copying one from the page and changing the year, rather than writing the layer codes by hand.
caveats: Settings of the workbench (open tab, chosen places) are not kept in the address.
A link names datasets by key. If a dataset is renamed or removed in a later version, its layer is dropped.

view.label: 2D map: poverty rate in 2022 as a shaded layer

values.<dataset>: The dataset key, for example poverty_pct or qcew_jobs. Unknown keys are ignored.
values.<mode>: f for a shaded layer, s for symbols.
values.<show-as>: One of the 'Show as' codes: value, per1000, perkm2, sharePR, shareJobs, lq, perCapita, index, diff, change, pctile. A code that the dataset does not offer becomes value.
values.<ramp>: blue, green, gold, red or gray.
values.<classes>: q for quantiles, e for equal intervals, j for natural breaks.
values.<fixed>: 1 for 'Same classes in every year', 0 for off.
values.<colour>: A number 0 to 4 for the symbol colour: 0 Red, 1 Blue, 2 Gold, 3 Green, 4 Charcoal.
values.ey: ey=<year>: the year. Left out when the year control is on 'Latest'.
values.eb: eb=<year>: the base year of 'Change measured from'. Left out when it is 2014.

name: Shareable link of the 3D view
plain: The 3D view reads two items from the page address: the camera centre and zoom (c) and a planned route (r). Layers and clocks are not kept in the address.
definition: The form is 3d.html#c=<lat>,<lng>,<zoom>&r=<lat>,<lng>;<lat>,<lng>. The zoom number is on the 2D map's scale: the 3D view subtracts 1 when it opens the link and adds 1 when it writes one. The 3D page writes the address when it opens and again whenever the route changes. It does not follow the camera as you move. The 'Map' link in the header carries the camera and route to the 2D map. An address with r= opens the Route tab and plans the route.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the page is updated.

method: twin3d.js (start, planHost.drawRoute, syncViewLinks).
how_to_read: Open the link to check it. Tilt and rotation are not in the link, so the camera opens at the page's usual angle. Example: 3d.html#c=18.4400,-66.0900,14 opens near the centre of San Juan.
caveats: The tilt, rotation, open tab, switches and the clock settings are not saved in the address.

The r= part holds the exact coordinates of every point of a planned route, to about 11 metres. If a start, end or stop is your home or workplace, anyone with the link can see it. Remove the r= part before you share a link, or use points that are not private.

view.label: 3D view: San Juan

name: Shareable link of the Housing page
plain: The Housing page keeps the municipality, the data year, the base year and an open dataset in the page address, so you can share the exact view.
definition: The form is housing.html?m=<municipality>&y=<year>&c=<base year>&d=<dataset>#<section>. The page updates the address when you pick a municipality, a year or a base year. It adds d when a 'Full data' dialog is open and removes it when the dialog closes. A link with d opens that dialog after the page has loaded. A link with an anchor scrolls to that section.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the page is updated.

method: housing.js (writeUrl, openDataset, init). The page reads the address once, when it loads.
how_to_read: Use d to point a reader at one dataset's full table, and y to fix the year. Example: housing.html?m=Ponce&y=2020&c=2014&d=median_gross_rent#profile opens the profile of Ponce for 2020, with changes measured from 2014, and the full table of median gross rent.
caveats: The page does not check that y is in range. Years after the latest data show the latest available value with a note.
The id table2 is not a valid d value. Use population for the population table.

view.label: Housing page: Ponce, 2020, with the rent table open

values.m: m=<municipality>: the municipality of the profile. Matched ignoring accents and capitals.
values.y: y=<year>: the data year (2010 to 2025 in Snapshot 2026-10). Left out for 'Latest'.

name: CSV and GeoJSON downloads
plain: Six buttons on the map and Housing pages save data as files: a municipality table, the places of a municipality, two economy tables, a housing table and a planned route. These files are made in your browser. The data dictionary page adds two more download buttons and a download link for each published data file.
definition: All comma-separated values (CSV) files are UTF-8 with a byte-order mark, so that Excel shows accents correctly. Cells are separated by commas, and text that holds a comma, a quote or a line break is put in quotes. A text cell that starts with =, +, - or @ gets a leading apostrophe, so that a spreadsheet does not run it as a formula. Empty cells mean no value. The buttons are listed below with the file each one saves.

coverage.frequency: Made from the data of the latest build each time you press the button.

method: app.js (downloadCsv), economy.js (ecSaveCsv), housing.js (saveCsv) and plan.js (download). On the dictionary page, dictionary.js (downloadSeries, downloadDictionary, saveCsv) does the same. Files are built in the browser and nothing is uploaded.
how_to_read: Cite the stored values in the files, not the rounded numbers on screen. Add the snapshot label and the date you downloaded them. A file has no citation of its own. Use the Cite button on the dictionary entries of the datasets it holds.
caveats: The files carry the licenses of their sources. Check each source's terms before you reuse or publish a file.
The places file can include helper columns whose names start with an underscore. They are search aids and can be ignored.
A file records what the page held when you pressed the button. Filters and settings on screen change what a places or table file holds.

One row for each of the 78 municipalities with every field of municipalities.json. Nested fields (places by category, land use in km²) become columns named with their parent. In Snapshot 2026-10 eight shares of places are blank for the 14 municipalities with no stop counted: transit_pct, acc_cur400_pct, acc_cur800_pct, acc_freq400_pct, acc_sat400_pct, acc_sun400_pct, acc_hub400_pct and acc_paper_pct. The other access fields (the stop counts by state, access_n and access_as_of) are included.
