The button loads the place listings first when they are not loaded yet (about 3.0 MB compressed in Snapshot 2026-10). One row for each place the map is showing in that municipality, so it follows the category buttons, the confidence slider and the worship switch. Columns are the fields of places.json and, when the access file has loaded, ts_m, ts_calls and ts_we of place_access.json. A column named id is never exported, and neither are socials, phone or email.
values.Download CSV (workbench table): Economy workbench, Table tab. File pr_economy_layers.csv. GEOID (the geographic identifier code of the Census Bureau), Municipality and one column for each visible layer, for the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico.
values.Download all years (CSV): Economy dataset dialog. File pr_economy_<dataset>.csv. GEOID, Municipality and one column for each year, with a margin-of-error column per year when the source publishes margins. Values as published.
values.Download CSV (Full data): Housing page, in a dataset's 'Full data' dialog. File pr_housing_<name>.csv. GEOID, Municipality and one column for each year, with a margin-of-error column per year when published. Published tables give their own rows. The Puerto Rico row has GEOID 72.
values.GeoJSON (route planner): Route planner. File planned_route.geojson. This is a GeoJSON file, not a CSV: the route line with a few results and one point for each chosen place.
values.Download all years (CSV), dictionary pag: Data dictionary page, on the entries that describe a yearly series (a field of economy_series.json or housing_series.json). File pr_digital_twin_<id>.csv, with each dot of the id turned into an underscore, for example pr_digital_twin_economy_qcew_jobs.csv. GEOID, Municipality and one column for each year, with a margin-of-error column per year when the source publishes margins. Values as published. The file has 79 rows: the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (GEOID 72).
values.Download the dictionary (CSV): Data dictionary page. File pr_digital_twin_data_dictionary.csv. One row for each entry, whatever the filters on the page, with these columns: id, name, area, group, kind, type, unit, geography, years, updates, plain description, definition, how it is computed, how to read it, cautions, sources, source detail, data fields, related entries and the date added.
values.Data file links, dictionary page: The data file names under 'Where it appears' on an entry and in the table of published data files are download links to the files themselves, as published in the data folder. These files are not made in your browser.

name: Data dictionary page: search, filters, citations and downloads
plain: The data dictionary page explains every dataset, variable, map layer and measure in the observatory: what it means, where it comes from, how it is worked out and what to watch out for. You can search it, filter it, copy a citation, download tables and read the sources, licenses and glossary.
definition: The page opens with a search box and four counts: documented items, data sources, glossary terms and published data files. 'Browse the dictionary' lists the entries by area and group. You can narrow the list with the search box and with these filters: area, source, kind (variable, map layer, published table, boundary, category, measure or method), time (one snapshot, every year, five-year windows, every ten years, by event, live, or not tied to a year), geography (the level of the published files an item describes), year covered, license of the sources (the strictest class among an item's sources) and 'Has margins of error'. A click on an entry opens it. An entry starts with a plain description and a list of facts: unit, type, geography, years, updates, area, kind and the date it was added. It then gives the definition, how it is computed, how to read it, cautions, codes, sources with their licenses, where it appears in the observatory (links to the views and to the data files you can download) and related entries. Three buttons end an entry: Cite, Copy link and, for yearly series, Download all years (CSV), which saves a file in comma-separated values (CSV) form. Four more sections follow the entries: Sources and licenses, Glossary, Published data files (a summary that links to the Data management page) and How to cite. The map, the 3D view and the Housing page each have a 'Data dictionary' link in their top bar.

coverage.frequency: dictionary.json and the files the page reads, made from it, are rewritten each time the dictionary is built, including at the end of a full build. registry.json is rewritten when the data are rebuilt. Numbers quoted in entries describe the snapshot named in the top bar.

method: dictionary.js builds the page in your browser. dictionary.py writes data/dictionary.json from the entry files, the source records and the glossary, with the names, units, years and sources that the economy and housing series catalogs already hold, and makes from it the files the page reads: data/dictionary_list.json, read first, with the list, the filters, the sources, the glossary and the words the search looks in, and data/dictionary_detail_<domain>.json, the rest of the entries of one top-level domain, fetched the first time one of them is opened (the entry says it is loading until then). Downloading the dictionary or printing the page fetches the detail files still missing. It also reads data/registry.json for the counts of the published data files and the geography level of each file, and the page works without it if the file does not load. The search removes accents and capitals from your words and keeps the entries that contain all of them. With a search the list is flat, and entries are sorted by how well the words match: a match in the name counts most, then the id, the group and the plain description. An entry's body is built the first time you open it. The filters are written into the page address as q, domain, source, kind, time, moe=1 and file, so you can share a filtered list.
source_detail: dictionary_list.json and the dictionary_detail files (made from dictionary.json), registry.json, economy_series.json and housing_series.json, read in your browser. Citations use the credit lines and licenses in the source records. The page draws no credit line of its own. Icons: Material Symbols (Google), Apache License 2.0.
how_to_read: Read the plain description first and then the cautions, which say what a number does not mean. Numbers quoted in entries come from the snapshot named in the top bar and change when the observatory is rebuilt. Definitions and methods do not. To cite a variable, open its entry and press Cite. To send a reader to an entry, press Copy link.
caveats: The page needs JavaScript. Without it the page shows a message and no entries.

Search needs every word to match. It looks in the id, name, area, group, kind, descriptions, method, unit, geography, source details, cautions and source names. It does not look in the codes tables, the related links or the glossary. A misspelt word finds nothing.

A citation names the snapshot and the original sources, and it uses the day you press Cite as the access date. The license text in the sources section is what each source states, not legal advice. Check the source's own terms before you reuse its data.
The page's introduction says the observatory uses public data, most of it under an open license. Not all: some sources state no license (the Data management page names them for each file).

A yearly-series file holds the values as published, with no inflation adjustment and no rescaling. A margin-of-error column appears only when the source publishes margins. A value the source does not give is an empty cell.
Print opens every entry in the current list and hides the top bar, the side panel, the filters and the buttons. A long list makes a long printout, so filter first.
Sizes of the published data files are in kilobytes of 1,024 bytes and megabytes of 1,048,576 bytes. Entries that give a size in megabytes of 1 million bytes read about 5% larger for the same file.

values.Search box: Type words such as poverty or flood. The list updates after a short pause. The x button empties the box.
values.Area: Ten areas, for example Housing, Hazards and environment or Map layers and tools. The same areas are buttons in the left column. Each choice shows how many items it holds.
values.Source: Every source that at least one item uses, with the number of items. The button 'Show the N dictionary items that use it' on a source card sets the same filter.
values.Kind: Variable, Map layer, Published table, Boundary, Category, Measure or Method. Only kinds that have items are listed.
values.Time: One snapshot, Every year, Five-year windows, Every ten years, By event, Live, or Not tied to a year. Only choices that have items are listed.
values.Geography: The level of the published data files that an item describes: whole island, municipality, barrio, census block, points (places and stops), lines (routes), areas or network. An item that describes no file (a method, for example) has none. Only levels that have items are listed, with the number of items.
values.Covers year: Keeps the items whose years include the year you pick. The list runs from 2000 to the snapshot year, with 'Before 2000' (storm tracks start in 1851) and 'Projections' (sea level scenarios run to 2100). A snapshot counts for its own year only.
values.License of the sources (strictest): Keeps the items whose most restrictive source has the class you pick: open, open with conditions, FPR's own, not stated, or licensed and not open. It describes the sources an item uses, as recorded in the sources list, not a legal review. Open the entry to see which source sets the class.
values.Has margins of error: Keeps only the series whose source publishes margins of error. In Snapshot 2026-10 all of them are American Community Survey series.
values.Data-file filter: On the Data management page, the link in the 'Documented by' column lists only the items that describe that file. The address then carries file=<name>. This filter has no menu of its own.
values.Reset filters: Clears the search and every filter, including the data-file filter.
values.Expand all and Collapse all: Expand all opens the first 60 entries of the list and says so when the list is longer. Collapse all closes every entry.
values.Cite: Opens a panel with four formats (Credit line, APA 7, Chicago and BibTeX) and a Copy button. The credit line names the sources and the snapshot. The APA 7, Chicago and BibTeX texts also give the address of the entry, the original sources and the date you pressed Cite. The panel repeats the credit lines of the sources underneath.
values.Copy link: Copies the address of the entry, for example dictionary.html#economy.qcew_jobs. The button then reads 'Link copied'.
values.Download all years (CSV): Only on the entries that describe a yearly series (a field of economy_series.json or housing_series.json). File pr_digital_twin_<id>.csv, with each dot of the id turned into an underscore. Columns: GEOID (the geographic identifier code), Municipality and one column for each year. A margin-of-error column follows each year when the source publishes margins. The file has 79 rows: the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (GEOID 72).
values.Download the dictionary (CSV): File pr_digital_twin_data_dictionary.csv, with one row for each entry whatever the filters on the page. See the entry on CSV and GeoJSON downloads for its columns.
values.Links that open an entry: dictionary.html#<id> opens that entry and scrolls to it, for example dictionary.html#economy.qcew_jobs. If a filter hides the entry, the filters are cleared first. An economy id that shares an entry with a housing series (for example economy.poverty_pct) opens the shared entry. Other anchors are #browse, #sources, #glossary, #files, #cite and #src-<source id> for one source card.
values.Sources and licenses: One card for each source: publisher, license or terms, credit line (with a Copy button), how the observatory gets the data, how often it changes, what the observatory uses it for, good to know, and when its link and license were last checked ('Link and license checked', 'Link works; license wording unclear', 'Link did not respond when checked' or 'Not yet checked'). A menu separates data sources from base maps, libraries and tools. 'Find a source' searches names, publishers, licenses, uses and credit lines.
values.Glossary: Terms, abbreviations and Spanish words in A to Z order, with a letter strip. Each term has a plain explanation and, where useful, links to entries.
values.Published data files: A summary of the files in the observatory's data folder: their number, total size and share of the hosting limit (1 gigabyte for a GitHub Pages site), and the records and values of the data files, with a link to the Data management page, which lists each file. A note below explains that the folder only grows.
values.How to cite: A citation of the observatory as a whole in the same four formats, and five points of good practice: name the snapshot, name the year of the data, keep the unit, share the view, and note that some data have extra terms.
values.Print: Prints every entry in the current list, opened, without the top bar, the side panel, the filters and the buttons. Entries avoid breaking across pages.

name: Data management page: published files, growth and what is not published
plain: The Data management page lists every data file the observatory publishes, with its records, fields, values, size, the dates it was first published and last updated, the dictionary items that document it and its compliance review. It also shows how the data grew over time and counts what is not published.
definition: The page opens with six figures: published files, size (with its share of the 1 GB GitHub Pages limit), records, values, documented items and the last update. The table of published data files has the columns File (a download link), What it holds, Domain, Records, Fields, Values, Size, First published, Last updated, Documented by (a link to the file's entries in the data dictionary) and Compliance review, a totals row for the files shown, a text filter, filters by kind and by review, sorting on every column and a download of what is shown as a comma-separated values (CSV) file. The Growth section draws one total at a time by date, with a table of every date. 'What is not published' gives counts only, each with its rule. The Definitions section defines record, field, value, vertex, size, the two dates, documented by, compliance review and the totals.

coverage.frequency: The page reads registry.json, which registry.py updates at every build and nightly transit refresh.

method: datamgmt.js builds the page in your browser from data/registry.json (registry.py and ledger.py). It loads no other data file.
source_detail: registry.json, read in your browser. Icons: Material Symbols (Google), Apache License 2.0.
how_to_read: Sort by Values to see where the data points are, by Last updated to see what changed recently and by Compliance review to see what still needs a review. The totals row adds the files shown. Records, fields and values are counted for data files only.
caveats: The page needs JavaScript. Without it the page shows a message.
Documentation and index files are listed and sized, not counted.
Sizes use 1 MB = 1,048,576 bytes.

The page is public and open to search engines (since 2026-10-20). It is read-only: it is generated from the observatory's repository at each build, and only the Foundation for Puerto Rico team can change the data, through reviewed changes.

name: 3D + Time view: scene, tabs and base map
plain: The 3D + Time view shows Puerto Rico as a tilted 3D scene with terrain and buildings, and three clocks: a day of transit, sea level by year and hurricanes since 1851.
definition: The top bar has the search box and links to the 2D map, the Housing page and the data dictionary. The side panel has four tabs: Layers, Time (the three clocks), Route (the route planner) and About. The About tab describes the view and links to the data dictionary (see the entry on the About tab). A time bar at the bottom switches between the clocks. The base map is the OpenFreeMap 'Liberty' style, which draws OpenStreetMap data; the 'Base map' choice, first in the 3D scene group of the Layers tab, switches to another OpenFreeMap style ('Positron', a light map for data; 'Bright'; 'Dark'; 'Fiord'), to a map of the USGS National Map (aerial imagery, topographic or shaded relief, draped over the terrain) or to no base map. A switch keeps every data layer, the terrain and the animated layers. The 3D buildings need OpenStreetMap's building tiles, so they are off on a USGS map and with no base map, and come back with an OpenFreeMap style; the counts on the clusters of stops need fonts, which every style but 'No base map' has. The choice is kept in the page address (bm=) and in the link to the 2D map, and remembered in this browser. The view needs WebGL, a browser feature for 3D graphics. Without it the page says so and points to the 2D map and the Housing page. The page opens on the whole island, tilted 50 degrees (35 on a phone). The codes below give the contents of the Map layers tab, the camera limits, what loads when and how the page behaves inside another page.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. Transit data are refreshed every night.

method: twin3d.js. MapLibre GL JS 4.7.1 draws the terrain, the buildings and the data layers, which follow the terrain. deck.gl 9.0.38 draws the animated layers (transit trips and storm tracks) over the map. The data are the same data files as on the 2D map.
source_detail: Credit line on the map, in the attribution box shared by every 3D layer: 'Places © Overture Maps Foundation · FEMA NFHL · NOAA (SLR, HURDAT2) · USGS PAD-US · US Census · ATI GTFS · © OpenStreetMap contributors · © OpenMapTiles · OpenFreeMap', followed by the terrain's own line (see the 3D terrain entry). In that line, FEMA NFHL is the National Flood Hazard Layer of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, NOAA is the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, SLR is sea level rise, HURDAT2 is the Atlantic hurricane database of the NOAA National Hurricane Center, AWS is Amazon Web Services, USGS PAD-US is the Protected Areas Database of the US Geological Survey, and ATI GTFS is the timetable data of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado in General Transit Feed Specification format.
how_to_read: Use the 3D view to see how places sit in the land. Use the 2D map for numbers, the Analysis tab and the chat.
caveats: The 3D view needs a recent browser with WebGL and downloads more data than the 2D map.
The 3D view has no confidence slider, no worship switch, no economy layers and no layer links. Its address keeps only the camera and a route.

The credit line names the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) for transit. Municipal feeds also supply routes, stops and trips in the 3D view, so credit them too when you cite. The route card names the right source.

view.label: 3D + Time view

values.Map layers tab: 3D scene (terrain and buildings), then the groups of the 2D map, in the same order and with the same layers where both views can draw them: Territory (municipal boundaries, barrios, columns by municipality), Hazards and environment, Land and housing (with public housing), Infrastructure and mobility (routes, stops, stations, taxi stands and EV charging, the walk rings, the vehicle replay), Community services (fire and EMS stations, police stations, city halls, public libraries, historic places), Communities and Visitor economy (tourism places).
values.Base map fallback: If the base map style cannot be loaded, the data layers appear on a plain background with a message.
values.Camera limits: The camera stays inside the box from 16.8 N to 19.6 N and from 69.5 W to 63.5 W, zooms out no further than level 5.5 and tilts up to 80 degrees.
values.Loading: In Snapshot 2026-10 the first screen loads the municipality statistics and boundaries, the routes, the stops and stations (transport.json), the operators and the service figures. The timetable replay and the storm tracks load after the first screen is drawn. The tourism places and every other layer load when you first switch them on.
values.Inside another page: When the page sits inside another page, the map takes two-finger gestures or Ctrl and scroll, so that the host page can still scroll.

name: 3D terrain, relief shading and exaggeration
plain: The '3D terrain' switch lifts the map into relief. The 'Terrain exaggeration' slider stretches the heights, from 1 to 3 times, so hills are easier to see.
definition: The switch is on at the start. The slider runs from 1× to 3× in steps of 0.1 and starts at 1.3×. It stretches heights for display. Light and dark relief shading (hillshade) is always on, at a fixed strength. The map also draws a sky and haze at the horizon. Heights come from elevation tiles in the Mapzen 'terrarium' format, served by Amazon Web Services (AWS) Open Data, which hold data up to zoom level 15. Beyond that level the tiles are enlarged. Data layers such as flood zones, routes and land use are draped on the relief.

coverage.frequency: Tiles are requested live while you browse.

method: twin3d.js (setupScene, setTerrain), with the terrain source, its Terrarium encoding and its credit read from site/js/core/basemap.js. The terrain source is https://s3.amazonaws.com/elevation-tiles-prod/terrarium.
source_detail: Credit line on the map: 'Terrain: Mapzen / AWS Open Data · 3DEP, SRTM and GMTED2010 data courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey · ETOPO1: NOAA', as the terrain tiles' attribution page asks.
how_to_read: Read the relief as a picture of the land. Do not read heights off the screen.
caveats: Exaggeration changes the picture, not the data. Slopes look steeper than they are above 1×.
The license of the elevation tiles is in the AWS Open Data registry entry. Check it before you reuse the tiles.

view.label: 3D + Time view: El Yunque

name: 3D buildings
plain: The '3D buildings' switch raises building footprints to the height stored in the OpenFreeMap map tiles, which draw OpenStreetMap data. A building with no height value is drawn 6 metres tall.
definition: The switch is on at the start. Buildings appear from zoom level 13. Each is a prism standing on the terrain. Its height is the render_height value in the OpenFreeMap tiles, and 6 metres where the tile has none. A building part raised above the ground starts at its minimum render height. Colour runs from light beige at 0 metres through grey-beige at 30 metres to darker brown-grey at 90 metres. Buildings are 85% opaque.

coverage.frequency: Tiles are requested live while you browse.

method: twin3d.js (setupScene): a fill-extrusion layer on the 'building' layer of the base map's vector tiles.
source_detail: Credit line on the map: '© OpenStreetMap contributors · © OpenMapTiles · OpenFreeMap'.
how_to_read: Use it to see the scale of the built area. A tall prism means a height value in the tile, not a measured height.
caveats: Buildings that nobody mapped are missing. A mapped building with no height value is drawn at the default 6 metres, so a tall building can look low.

The heights come from the OpenFreeMap tiles. The observatory has not checked how OpenFreeMap sets the render_height value, so it cannot say whether a height was recorded by volunteers or estimated. The heights are not surveyed and must not be used for engineering.

name: 3D view: moving around, quick views and buttons
plain: You move the 3D view with the mouse, with touch, with the keyboard or with the buttons at the right. Four quick-view buttons fly to San Juan, El Yunque, Ponce and the whole island.
definition: The 3D view has four ways to move: the mouse, touch, the keyboard and the buttons at the right. The codes below describe each way and the four quick views. Letter keys steer the map only when nothing else has the focus.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the page is updated.

how_to_read: Press the keyboard button in the controls to see these keys in the page.
caveats: Keyboard keys need the map or the page to have the focus. A key typed in a box does nothing to the map.

values.Touch: One finger pans, two fingers zoom and rotate, and two fingers dragged up or down together tilt.

name: 3D view: Places layer
plain: The 3D 'Tourism places' layer shows tourism places as a heat map from far away and as coloured points when you zoom in. Four category buttons filter them.
definition: The layer holds the same places as the 2D map with confidence 0.50 or more and no places of worship (23,467 with a pin in Snapshot 2026-10, shown beside the switch once loaded; holiday rentals are counted but not drawn). The layer starts switched off: its file (about 2.8 MB compressed) loads the first time it is switched on, and from then the place search also lists tourism places. The 'Render as' menu offers 'Heat at island scale, points when zoomed' (start), 'Points' and 'Heat'. Points show from zoom level 10.5 (everywhere in 'Points' mode), grow as you zoom and take the category colour. A point inside a Special Flood Hazard Area of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) has a dark blue rim. The heat map adds one unit for each place and fades out between zoom levels 11 and 13. A click on a point opens a card with the name, the type, the municipality, the flood zone when the place is in a hazard area, the access badge and the distance to the nearest stop with a current timetable (the same lines as the 2D pop-up), and the credit 'Overture Maps'.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. Transit data are refreshed every night.

method: twin3d.js (addPlaces, updatePlacesMode, placesFilter). The filter keeps places of the chosen categories, with a confidence of at least 0.50, that are not places of worship.
source_detail: places.json. Credit line on the map: 'Places © Overture Maps Foundation'.
how_to_read: Use the heat to see where visitor places cluster. Use the points to see single places.
caveats: In 'Heat' mode the heat fades out between zoom levels 11 and 13, so a close-up shows no places.
Overture listings can be missing, duplicated or out of date. The 3D view has no confidence slider and no worship switch.
The 3D view does not recalculate flags when you change a button. The rim and the card come from the build and from the stored access columns.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Places layer, San Juan

name: 3D view: Columns by municipality
plain: 'Columns by municipality' raises each municipality into a column whose height shows one measure. The menu has 33 measures (the 35 of the 2D map's shading less its three 'shown' measures, plus population change 2010 to 2020) and any dataset of the Analysis tab. The columns start off.
definition: With a measure chosen, each municipality rises as a column standing on its own area. The column height is proportional to the value, starting at zero. The largest value reaches 14,000 display metres (12,000 for population change). These are map heights, not real heights. Colour follows five groups of about equal size, in the same light-to-dark blue as the 2D map. The legend under the menu shows three numbers: the lowest value, the second class limit (the value two fifths of the way along the sorted list) and the highest value. A click on a column, or on the municipality when columns are off, opens a card with a link to the 2D map. The codes below list the 33 measures and the card. A yes/no measure (whether Uber lists the municipality) raises the listed municipalities to one height and leaves the others as a flat grey sheet; rent change, which can fall, uses the red-to-blue scale of population change.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. Transit data are refreshed every night.

method: twin3d.js (METRIC, setMetric, addMunicipalities). The menu lists the fields below.
how_to_read: Read heights as 'more or less than other municipalities'. The tallest column is the largest value, not a target.
caveats: A value that equals a class limit takes the lower class in both the 3D view and the 2D map. The limits themselves can still differ for the shares of places near stops (see the caveat on municipalities with no stop counted).

In Snapshot 2026-10, 14 municipalities have no stop counted. The 3D view uses the stored shares of places near stops (any mapped stop, a stop with a current timetable, a frequent stop, only an expired or unscheduled stop) for every municipality, in the columns and on the card. For those 14 the stored value is 0% or close to it (0.5% for Toa Alta and 0.9% for Arroyo, for the shares near any mapped stop and near a stop with a current timetable), which means not measured. The 2D map leaves those 14 unshaded for those shares and works out their class limits from the other 64 municipalities, while 3D keeps all 78 in the limits, so the limits and a few colours of these shares can differ between the two views.
Tall columns hide what is behind them. Rotate or tilt the view.

Heights start at zero, so a column twice as tall is not twice as different when the values of all municipalities are close together. In Snapshot 2026-10 the affordability ratio, for example, runs only from 0.97 to 1.92.

When many municipalities share a value, several class limits are equal, and the classes between them stay empty, as in the 2D map. In Snapshot 2026-10 this happens for the measure 'Transit: % of residents within 400 m of a scheduled stop (incl. expired timetables)' (40 of the 78 municipalities have 0%), for residents near a stop with a current timetable (46 at 0%) and for the shares of places near a stop with a current timetable (47), near a frequent stop (59) and near only an expired or unscheduled stop (33). The legend then repeats a number (for the first of these measures it reads 0%, 0% and 81%), but the colours and the heights follow the measure.

name: 3D view: flood zones and sea level switches
plain: In the 3D group Hazards and environment, 'Flood zones' drapes the flood zones of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) on the terrain. 'Sea level rise' draws a sea level layer whose height comes from the Time tab. Both are off when the page opens.
definition: Flood zones are filled at 45% opacity with the same four colours as the 2D map. Red is for floodways, darkest blue for V and VE zones, mid blue for other Special Flood Hazard Area zones and light blue for the 0.2% annual chance zone. A click opens the 2D map's section for up to two zones under the click: the zone, whether it is a Special Flood Hazard Area (1% annual chance) or a 0.2% annual chance zone, the subtype spelled out and the credit 'FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer'. Where other areas are under the click too (land use, a protected area, a Comunidad Especial, a barrio), the same card has a section for each, as on the 2D map. The flood file (about 8 MB) downloads the first time you switch it on. The 'Sea level rise' switch draws the tile layer of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) at 70% opacity below the flood zones. The label beside it gives the feet and the year, for example '1 ft · 2050' (the start setting: Intermediate scenario, year 2050). The height comes from the year and scenario set in the Time tab. Choosing the Years clock switches this layer on by itself.

coverage.frequency: Flood zones are rebuilt with each snapshot. Sea level tiles are requested live from NOAA.

method: twin3d.js (addFlood, setSlr, currentFeet); the card's section is floodPopup in access.js, which both views share. The flood filter keeps polygons in the Special Flood Hazard Area or in the 0.2% zone.
source_detail: flood.geojson. The sea level tiles are streamed live from NOAA, and the year and scenario curves are typed into the page code. Credit lines on the map: 'FEMA NFHL' and 'Sea level rise: NOAA OCM' (the NOAA Office for Coastal Management).
how_to_read: Read the flood zones as FEMA's mapped hazard. Read the sea level layer as a what-if at the chosen height.
caveats: Flood zones are mapped hazards, not predictions. They say nothing about a building's elevation or insurance.
The sea level layer is a screening tool. It is not a forecast for a year. See the sea level entries.
If NOAA's tiles do not answer, a message appears and the layer stays empty.

The flood zones are a simplified copy of FEMA's data for context. FEMA's printed flood maps and Flood Insurance Study are the official designation. This is not a flood determination for any property. Read the source's terms before you rely on it.

NOAA says the sea level layer shows water at the highest high tides and does not model storm surge, erosion, subsidence or new construction. NOAA calls it a planning reference that should not be used for navigation, permitting or other legal purposes.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Layers tab, Hazards

name: 3D view: transit routes, stops, stations and taxi stands
plain: The 3D Mobility section draws transit routes (on at the start) and, if you switch them on, stops, stations, terminals and airports, taxi stands and EV chargers and the 400 m walk rings, as the 2D map does. Another switch controls the vehicle replay.
definition: Routes use the operator colours of the 2D map: Tren Urbano red (4 pixels), buses of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) blue, municipal systems green, públicos gold and ferries teal (2.5 pixels). All other lines are 2 pixels. Dashed lines mean the feed lists stops out of order. Dotted lines mean no road path was found. Width does not change with trips. A click opens a card with the route name, the operator, the route label, weekday trips, how the line was drawn and the credit. Stations show as dots: Tren Urbano red, ferry terminals teal, bus stations and airports charcoal, with airports slightly larger. A click on a station opens the same card as on the 2D map (name, kind, municipality, routes, modes, departures, timetable dates, operator and source). Stops, taxi stands and EV chargers and the walk rings are the 2D map's layers, with the same cards: see the entries of their switches, which both views share.

coverage.frequency: Feeds are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time.

method: twin3d.js (addRoutes, addHubs, addStops, addTaxi, addRings). The files are transit_routes.geojson and transport.json; the cards are transportPopup in access.js.
how_to_read: Compare the line style with the 2D legend to see how a line was drawn.
caveats: Routes of operators whose timetable has expired stay on the map.
A route in a feed is not proof that the service runs today.

The credit line on the map names the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) only. In Snapshot 2026-10, municipal feeds supply most routes: 127 of the 165 routes are not ATI routes, and 111 of them are municipal. The route card names the right source (ATI, a municipal feed or OpenStreetMap). The station card names its source, as on the 2D map. Of the 145 stations, terminals and airports in Snapshot 2026-10, 29 bus stations come from municipal feeds, 65 points (47 bus stations, 7 ferry terminals and 11 airports) from OpenStreetMap and 14 airports from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Credit those sources too when you cite.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Layers tab, Mobility

source_detail: transit_routes.geojson (routes) and transport.json (kinds bus_station, rail_station, ferry_terminal and airport). The shared attribution box on the map names, for transit, 'ATI GTFS' (the timetable data of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, in General Transit Feed Specification format) and 'OpenFreeMap © OpenStreetMap contributors'.

name: 3D view: land use and protected areas
plain: The 3D view can drape the Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 and the protected areas of the US Geological Survey (USGS) on the terrain. Both are off when the page opens.
definition: Land use is drawn from the class colours stored in the file at 45% opacity, with water and road polygons left out. A click opens the 2D map's section: the class name, code and municipio, and the credit. In Snapshot 2026-10 the land-use file is about 17.7 MB and loads the first time you switch the layer on. Protected areas are green at 35% opacity with a dark green outline. A click opens the 2D map's section for up to two records under the click: the name, the designation spelled out (Local Park for LP, for example; a code the card does not know is shown as stored), the manager, the public access, the acres and the Gap Analysis Project (GAP) status. Overlapping areas share one card, with a section for each, as on the 2D map.

coverage.frequency: Land use is the plan version of 30 November 2015. Protected areas are PAD-US 4.1.

method: twin3d.js (addLanduse, addProtected); the card's sections are landusePopup and protPopup in access.js, which both views share.
source_detail: landuse.geojson and protected.geojson. Credit lines on the map: 'Junta de Planificación' for land use and 'USGS PAD-US' for protected areas (PAD-US is the Protected Areas Database of the United States).
how_to_read: Use the drape to see the pattern. For the full meaning of a code, read the dictionary entry.
caveats: The land-use plan is a planning classification, not zoning, and dates from 2015.
'Protected' has a wide meaning. It includes recreation areas and military land.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Layers tab, Land use and Protected areas

name: 3D view: the time bar and the three clocks
plain: A bar at the bottom of the 3D view has a play button, a label, a slider and three buttons that choose the clock: Day, Years or Storms.
definition: Day: the slider runs from 00:00 to 23:59 in one-minute steps and the label reads like '07:00 · weekday transit'. Years: the slider runs from 2020 to 2150 in steps of 5 and the label reads like '2050 · Intermediate sea level'. Storms: the slider runs over the storm window and the label reads like '2024 · storms, trailing 10 years'. The window is the chosen year and the 10 years before it (11 calendar years). Choosing Years switches the sea level layer on. Choosing Storms switches the storm tracks on. Leaving Years switches off a sea level layer that Years switched on, but not one you switched on yourself. Play advances the Day clock at the chosen speed, the Years clock by 12 years each second and the Storms clock by 4 years each second. The Years and Storms clocks stop at their end. The Day clock wraps around at midnight. The Time tab in the side panel has the same controls with explanations. The three clocks are independent: each keeps its own value.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the page is updated.

method: twin3d.js (setMode, tick, togglePlay, syncClock). Animation uses the browser's frame timer. A long pause between frames (for example a background tab) counts as at most a quarter of a second of play.
how_to_read: Press Play on a clock, then change the clock with the buttons to compare.
caveats: The clocks do not move together. The Day clock is a time of day, not a date.

view.label: 3D + Time view: time bar

values.Day: The transit replay clock. See 'A day of transit'.
values.Years: The sea level clock. See 'Sea level by year'.

name: 3D view: A day of transit (scheduled vehicles)
plain: 'A day of transit' replays every scheduled weekday trip of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and municipal timetables as a coloured trail that moves across the map. It is a timetable replay, not tracking by Global Positioning System (GPS).
definition: The switch 'Scheduled vehicles' is on at the start. The clock runs from 00:00 to 23:59 and starts at 07:00. Speeds are 30×, 60× (one minute of clock each second, the start setting), 180× and 600×. The clock wraps around at midnight. A trail shows the last 7 minutes of each trip, fading behind the head. The colours are red for the Tren Urbano, gold for ATI buses, green for municipal buses and teal for ferries. These are not the route colours of the 3D map, where ATI buses are blue. The label beside the controls says 'N vehicles in service', counted once a minute of the clock as trips whose first stop time is at or before the clock and whose last stop time is at or after it. On a computer the replay starts by itself. On a phone, or when your device asks for reduced motion, it waits for Play.

coverage.frequency: Timetables are re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time.

method: twin3d.js (tripsLayer, tickBody). deck.gl draws the TripsLayer from trips.json, the weekday file of a typical Wednesday (3,297 trips from 25 operators in Snapshot 2026-10). Each trail follows its trip's route line (the operator's shape, or the roads the route is snapped to), timed between the stops that have a scheduled time (tripPoints in common.js). In Snapshot 2026-10, 3,191 of the 3,297 trips follow their route line; 106 whose stops fit no line of their route run in straight lines between stops.
how_to_read: Read the trails as where the timetable says vehicles are at that time. A quiet map at night is a quiet timetable.
caveats: The replay includes trips of operators whose timetable has expired. In Snapshot 2026-10, 372 of the 3,297 weekday trips belong to operators whose feed had ended by the build date. The 2D map leaves them out.
Only the weekday file is used. The Saturday and Sunday files are not replayed in 3D, and holidays are not modelled.
No public real-time bus feed exists, so late or cancelled vehicles run on time here.
The credit line on the map names ATI only. In Snapshot 2026-10, 1,168 of the 3,297 weekday trips come from municipal feeds (ATI has 2,129), so credit the municipalities too when you cite.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Time tab, A day of transit

source_detail: trips.json, Snapshot 2026-10: the weekday file, a typical Wednesday, with 3,297 trips. The shared attribution box on the map names 'ATI GTFS' (the timetable data of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, in General Transit Feed Specification format). The trails carry no credit line of their own.

name: 3D view: Sea level by year
plain: The 'Sea level by year' controls turn a year and a scenario of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) into the sea level layer. Pick a year from 2020 to 2150 and one of four scenarios, and the map shows the matching NOAA layer.
definition: The year slider runs from 2020 to 2150 in steps of 5 and starts at 2050. The scenario menu offers Intermediate-Low, Intermediate (start), Intermediate-High and High, the NOAA 2022 scenarios. A note says, for example, '2050 · Intermediate ≈ 1.0 ft (0.30 m) above the 2000 baseline → showing the NOAA 1 ft layer'. The height is rounded to whole feet and held between 1 and 10 feet. Moving either control swaps the layer when the height in whole feet changes. Play moves the year forward 12 years each second until 2150, then stops. Pressing Play again at 2150 restarts at 2020. Playing needs the Years clock, and choosing it switches the layer on.

coverage.frequency: NOAA's tiles are requested live. The scenario curves are fixed in the page code.

method: twin3d.js (currentFeet, setSlr, the year and scenario handlers). The conversion from year and scenario to feet is described in the entry 'Sea level rise by year and scenario'.
how_to_read: Read a year as a position on a scenario curve. Several years show the same layer, because heights are rounded to whole feet.
caveats: The curves are global average sea level above the 2000 level, read approximately from the tables of NOAA's 2022 report and typed into the page. They are not NOAA's published values for Puerto Rico.
The map is a what-if at a height, not a forecast for a year.
The note on the page calls the scenarios 'planning what-ifs'.
The layer never shows less than 1 ft, so the first years show more water than the scenario gives (see the entry 'Sea level rise by year and scenario').
The layer never shows more than 10 ft, so the highest part of the High scenario is capped (see the same entry).

NOAA says the sea level layer shows water at the highest high tides and does not model storm surge, erosion, subsidence or new construction. NOAA calls it a planning reference that should not be used for navigation, permitting or other legal purposes.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Time tab, Sea level by year

values.Scenario curves: The four curves (metres above the 2000 level for 2020, 2050, 2100 and 2150) are listed in the entry 'Sea level rise by year and scenario'.

source_detail: twin3d.js, SCENARIOS: the curves, typed into the page from NOAA's 2022 report (no data file). The layer itself is NOAA's tile service. Credit line on the map: 'Sea level rise: NOAA OCM' (the NOAA Office for Coastal Management).

name: 3D view: Hurricane controls
plain: The Hurricane controls draw the tracks of storms that came within 250 kilometres of Puerto Rico since 1851. You can filter by years and strength, play them through time and open any storm from a list.
definition: The switch 'Storm tracks within 250 km' is off at the start and shows the number of storms drawn. Two sliders set a year window from 1851 to 2025 (all years at the start). The menu 'Minimum category near PR' (Puerto Rico) offers All (including tropical storms), Hurricane (Category 1 or more), Major (Category 3 or more, the start setting) and Category 4 or more. In Snapshot 2026-10, at the start (Major), the map shows 29 of the 157 storms. Lines are coloured by the category near the island, and line width grows with the category. Dots mark recorded positions, coloured and sized by wind. Pointing at a line shows the name, the year, the category near Puerto Rico, the peak wind in knots and the closest approach in kilometres; a click on a line shows the same in a card (on a phone, which has no pointing). 'Strongest in window' lists up to 25 storms by category, then wind, then newest. A click on a row fits the map to that storm's whole track.
geography: Atlantic storms within 250 km of Puerto Rico

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. NOAA adds each season after it ends.

method: twin3d.js (stormsLayers, renderStormList, tickBody). deck.gl draws the lines and dots from hurricanes.json.
source_detail: hurricanes.json, Snapshot 2026-10: 157 storms from 1851 to 2025. Credit line on the map: 'NOAA (SLR, HURDAT2)'. NOAA is the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, SLR is sea level rise and HURDAT2 is the Atlantic hurricane database of the NOAA National Hurricane Center.
how_to_read: Thicker, darker lines are stronger near the island. A long line is the whole track, which can reach far from Puerto Rico.
caveats: Old tracks and winds are less certain than recent ones. Counts by decade are not a trend.
Lines join recorded positions with straight segments.
The list and the card label every category 0 storm 'Tropical storm'.
The minimum-category menu has no Category 2 or more choice.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Time tab, Hurricanes 1851–2025

values.0: Category 0, grey: tropical storm or depression strength near the island. 92 storms in Snapshot 2026-10.
values.5: Category 5, dark red. 5 storms in Snapshot 2026-10.
values.Play through the years: Moves a year forward 4 times each second and shows the storms of the chosen year and the 10 years before it (11 calendar years), with older ones fading. Dragging a window slider returns to the whole window.

name: 3D view: route planner and fly-along
plain: The Route tab of the 3D view plans a route like the 2D planner, drapes it on the terrain and can fly the camera along it.
definition: The boxes, buttons and results are the same as in the 2D planner. The route is drawn as a dark line with a white edge. A leg that cannot follow roads is a red dotted line. Lettered markers can be dragged. After a route is planned a button 'Fly along the route' appears. The camera then follows the line at tilt 64 degrees and zoom 14.8, turning to face ahead, and covers the route in about 45 seconds, at a speed between 120 and 1,500 metres per second. A mouse press, a touch, the wheel or Escape stops the flight, and the button reads 'Stop flying' while it runs. If your device asks for reduced motion, the flight does not start and a message says why. The chosen points are kept in the page address as r=.

coverage.frequency: Computed in your browser each time you plan a route.

method: twin3d.js (planHost, flyAlong) with plan.js. The route is drawn as fresh map layers each time it changes, and the routes layer is refreshed so that the whole route shows on the terrain.
how_to_read: Fly along a route to see what it passes. Read the numbers on the card with the 2D planner's entries.
caveats: A flight is a visual aid. It is not a drive time. The running time on the card uses planning speeds.
The planner's other limits apply. See the route planner entry.

The address holds the exact coordinates of every point, to about 11 metres. If a start, end or stop is your home or workplace, anyone with the link can see it. Remove the r= part before you share a link, or use points that are not private.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Route tab with an example route

name: Housing page: sections, tags and data years
plain: The Housing page reproduces key tables of the 2023 study 'The State of Housing in Puerto Rico' by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR), as printed. It also adds live data for all 78 municipalities, 2010 to 2025 in Snapshot 2026-10. The live data come from Census Bureau population estimates (through 2025), American Community Survey (ACS) windows (through 2020-2024) and housing assistance figures from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).
definition: A contents bar lists 13 sections: Headline, Population, Housing stock, Cost burden, Affordability, Ownership, Rent and value change, Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC), Recovery, Municipality profile, Land use, Data and Sources. A year bar below it moves every map, chart and table. The page holds 28 maps, each with a ranked chart, plus charts and tables. Maps and charts are built when you scroll near them. Published figures carry the tag 'study'. Live figures carry the Census Bureau's survey and year, shown as tags, listed below. A click on a municipality on any map loads its profile. A sources section lists every source with its license and the way to cite the page. Without JavaScript the page cannot draw its maps, charts and tables. The top bar links to the 2D map, the 3D view and the data dictionary, and the 'Full data' window of a series links to that series' entry in the dictionary.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: housing.js reads data/housing_series.json (built by housing_series.py), housing.json (the study's tables), municipalities.json and municipios.geojson. Charts use Chart.js and the maps use Leaflet, without a base map.
how_to_read: Check the tag before you cite a figure. A 'study' tag means printed in 2023. A survey tag means a live figure for that window.
caveats: The page reproduces Tables 2, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 and the headline figures of the study as printed. Other tables of the study are not reproduced as printed here. The entry on published tables gives the details.
The table numbers are those used on this page and in this dictionary. The study PDF numbers some tables differently (for example the affordability table is Table 8 in the PDF and Table 6 here).

view.label: Housing page
Housing page: Headline

values.Census 2020: Tag on an April 1 figure. For housing units and for the 2010 population it is the census count. For population in 2020 it is the Census Bureau's April 1, 2020 estimates base, not the census file (see the entry on resident population).

The maps on this page have no base map and carry no credit line. The tag beside each title names the source.

name: Knowledge Area: its areas, its home page and the header of each page
plain: The Knowledge Area gathers Foundation for Puerto Rico's research and program tools, a home page that lists them all and a header on each page with an 'All areas' menu: Housing, WCRP, Route analysis, Global Innovation Index, Women in the labor force, How public money moves, FEMA disaster funding and need, Budget and public spending, Federal grants: balances, reductions and audit findings, Urban heat, Inflation, Reservoirs, Broadband gaps, Energy, Opportunity Zones 2.0 and Connections between municipios. WCRP, Route analysis, Global Innovation Index, FEMA disaster funding and need, Budget and public spending, Federal grants: balances, reductions and audit findings, Urban heat, Inflation, Reservoirs, Broadband gaps, Energy and Connections between municipios keep a small 'In review' marker in the menu and on their page, with a notice at the top, because their content may still change.
definition: The 'Knowledge' button of the top bar opens the Knowledge home page (knowledge.html): one card for every published area, grouped by topic, with its kind (FPR study, analysis, program tool or index profile), whether it is in review and by whom, the month it was updated, the other topics it belongs to and the published datasets it uses, with a search box and filters. On each area page, the bar below the top bar starts with a header: 'Knowledge' (back to the home page), the area's topic (it opens that topic on the map), an 'All areas' menu that lists every area that is not hidden, grouped by topic, whether the area is in review and by whom, and the month it was updated; the page's own sections follow. The areas, in the order of the menu: Housing (housing.html, published), WCRP (wcrp.html, published, marked 'In review'), Route analysis (route-analysis.html, published, marked 'In review') Global Innovation Index (gii.html, published, marked 'In review'), Women in the labor force (women-labor.html, published), FEMA disaster funding and need (public-money.html, published, marked 'In review'), Budget and public spending (public-spending.html, published, marked 'In review'), Federal grants: balances, reductions and audit findings (unused-funds.html, published, marked 'In review'), Urban heat (urban-heat.html, published, marked 'In review'), Inflation (inflation.html, published, marked 'In review', under Economy), Reservoirs (reservoirs.html, published, marked 'In review', under Infrastructure), Broadband gaps (broadband.html, published, marked 'In review', under Infrastructure), Energy (energy.html, published, marked 'In review', under Infrastructure), Opportunity Zones 2.0 (opportunity-zones.html, published, under Economy) and Connections between municipios (transit-links.html, published, marked 'In review', under Infrastructure). The tab of the page you are on is highlighted. A tab in review carries the marker 'In review'. The page of an area in review shows only a short message that the area is in review, with links to Housing and to the map, and asks search engines not to index it. A published area may keep the marker for a while after its content is approved: its page shows its content with a notice at the top that it is in review and may change, and it also asks search engines not to index it. An area is published (with or without the marker), in review or hidden (no tab).

A new area needs one entry in that list and its page.

name: Housing page: year bar and base year
plain: The year bar at the top of the Housing page moves every map, chart and table to the chosen year. 'Change measured from' sets the base year for the change maps.
definition: The bar has previous and next buttons, a year list ('Latest', then 2025 down to 2010 in Snapshot 2026-10), a slider over the same years and a Play button. Play starts at 2010, or at the chosen year, moves one year every 1.3 seconds up to the last year and stops. Choosing a year by hand stops it. Changing the base year does not. In Snapshot 2026-10 the base year list holds 2010 to 2023 and starts at 2012. It sets the base of the change maps and the change rows of the profile. Each dataset shows the same year when it has one, otherwise its latest earlier year (the chip says 'latest at or before 2021') or, if the year is before it starts, its first year (the chip says 'first data'). The published tables as printed and the land-use maps (a 2015 plan) do not change with the year. The year, the base year and the municipality are kept in the page address.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: housing.js (initYearBar, setYear, setBase, resolve, writeUrl).
how_to_read: Read the chip next to a map title for the year it really shows.
caveats: American Community Survey (ACS) years are five-year windows labelled by their last year. Neighbouring windows share four of five years of sample, so compare windows that do not overlap (2012, 2017, 2022) for real change.
In Snapshot 2026-10 the 2021–2025 window is not published yet (the page expects it in December 2026), so 2025 shows the 2020-2024 window for ACS data.

Population is the 2010 census count (April 1, 2010), the April 1, 2020 base of the Census Bureau's latest estimates (the page tags it 'Census 2020') and July 1 estimates in other years. The 2020 base equals the census count for the island but differs from it by 1 to 31 people in 68 of the 78 municipalities in the 2026-10 snapshot.

view.label: Housing page: year 2020, base 2014

values.Note beside the bar: For 'Latest' it names each dataset's own latest year (population 2025, ACS 2020-2024). For a year after the latest survey it says that the ACS window for that year is not published yet, that the maps show 2020-2024, and that population is that year's estimate. For any other year it gives the ACS window that ends in it and the July 1 population estimate.

name: Housing page: maps and ranked charts
plain: Each housing variable has a map of the 78 municipalities and a ranked bar chart. Colours show five groups whose limits come from all years together, so the same colour means the same number in every year.
definition: Each block has a title with a year chip, the source tag, a '?' help button and a 'Full data' button. A line gives the median, lowest and highest of the 78 municipalities and the Puerto Rico value. Below are a map, a readout for the selected municipality with its rank, a bar chart of all 78 municipalities (highest first) and a legend with the number of municipalities in each class. The class limits are the quintiles of the 78 municipalities over every year of the variable together, except on the five diverging maps (see the codes below). Because of that, the groups are not equal in size in one year: in Snapshot 2026-10, for median gross rent in 2024, the five groups hold 1, 3, 9, 26 and 39 municipalities. Municipalities with no value are pale grey. The maps have no base map, do not zoom with the wheel and, on a touch device, do not drag. The codes below list the 28 maps by section, the diverging maps and the selection.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: housing.js (buildViz, updateViz, pooled, colorFor, legendHTML). A map is built when it comes within about 800 pixels of the screen.
how_to_read: Read the legend for the numbers. The colour classes do not change with the year, so a municipality can change colour as its value moves.
caveats: Ranks and medians count only municipalities with a value. Tied values share the first of their places.
Survey estimates for small municipalities carry large margins of error. The readout shows the margin (±) when the survey publishes one.

view.label: Housing page: Home ownership affordability

values.Selection and hover: A click on a municipality on the map, or on a bar, selects it. The selected municipality is outlined in dark grey on every map, and the profile and readouts follow. Pointing at a municipality shows its name, value, rank and the source tag.
values.Diverging maps: Five maps use a diverging scale around 0: the four change maps (home value, gross rent, household income and bachelor's share) and the population-change map. The class limits are −50%, −10%, +10% and +50% of the largest absolute value over all years: below −50%, −50% to −10%, within ±10%, +10% to +50% and above +50% of that value. For population change the largest value is 39.05% in the 2026-10 snapshot. Blue is an increase and red is a decrease. Neither means better or worse. The limits of the four change maps depend on the base year chosen in the year bar.
values.Section 2, housing stock: vacancy_pct, other_vacant_pct, seasonal_pct, rental_vacancy_pct, overcrowded_pct, residents_per_unit.
values.Section 6, short-term rentals and the ma: The four change maps: gross_rent_change_pct, home_value_change_pct, income_change_pct, bachelors_change_pts. They are calculated in your browser from the survey series and follow the base year. They share names with fields of municipalities.json, which use a fixed base.
values.Section 10, land use: urban_pct, urbanizable_pct, protected_land_pct. These read municipalities.json and show one year, 2015.

source_detail: housing_series.json (the 21 survey, census, estimate and recovery series, and the four change maps calculated from them), municipalities.json (the three land-use maps) and municipios.geojson (the outlines). The maps have no base map and carry no credit line. The tag beside each title names the source.

name: Housing page: change since the base year
plain: Four maps on the Housing page show change since a base year. They cover median home value, median gross rent, median household income and the share of adults with a bachelor's degree.
definition: For home value, rent and income the value is the percent change: (value in the selected year minus value in the base year) divided by the value in the base year, times 100, rounded to two decimals. For the bachelor's share it is the difference in percentage points. Dollars are not adjusted for inflation. The base year is chosen in the year bar and starts at 2012, the window 2008-2012. Only years after the base year have a value. The page calls these maps 'change, base → year'. The same numbers fill the change rows of the municipality profile.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: housing.js (CHANGE, indexSeries). The values are calculated in the browser from the American Community Survey (ACS) series, so they follow the base year.
how_to_read: A positive percentage means the value rose in dollars of its own year. Part of a rise in prices or rents is general inflation.
caveats: Not inflation-adjusted. Use the Analysis tab's inflation option for constant dollars.
Windows that overlap share most of their sample. Pick a base year at least five years before the selected year for real change.
The change fields in the municipality statistics use a fixed base of 2008-2012 and the latest window. These maps follow the base you choose.

view.label: Housing page: change in rent, base 2012, 2022

source_detail: housing_series.json (median_home_value, median_gross_rent, median_hh_income and bachelors_pct, calculated in your browser) and municipios.geojson. The maps have no credit line. The tag beside each title names the source.

name: Housing page: 'Full data' window
plain: A 'Full data' window shows one dataset in full. It lists every municipality and Puerto Rico, every year and the margins of error where published. It has a trend chart and a download of the data as a comma-separated values (CSV) file.
definition: Open it with a 'Full data' button, a latest-data number, a row label in the profile, a dataset in the catalog or the link ?d=. The window shows tags, the definition, the source (linked), the table reference and a note on the years (American Community Survey (ACS) windows, the population basis or the disasters of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, FEMA). It adds a note on margins of error (±, 90% confidence) and, for a series, a 'Full entry' link to its entry in the data dictionary. Published tables open the same window with their rows and a CSV file. The file is pr_housing_<name>.csv. The codes below describe the tools, the chart and the table.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: housing.js (openDataset, openStatic, renderDsTable, renderDsChart, dsCsv). The address gets ?d=<dataset> while the dialog is open.
how_to_read: Use the window to find the exact value and its margin. Cite the value with its survey window.
caveats: Italics warn of low reliability. They are shown whether or not margins are switched on.

view.label: Housing page: median gross rent, full data

values.Tools: A box to find a municipality, a switch 'Show margin of error (±)', the count of municipalities and years, and 'Download CSV'.
values.Trend chart: Draws the ticked municipalities (up to 8). Puerto Rico and the selected municipality are ticked at the start.
values.Table: Puerto Rico first, then the 78 municipalities by name, one column for each year. A click on a column heading sorts by it. The column of the selected year is highlighted. A value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate is shown in italics.

name: Housing page: municipality profile (Table 11 for any municipality)
plain: The Municipality profile shows the study's Table 11 variables and the housing indicators for any municipality and year. Pick one from the menu or click any map.
definition: The menu lists the 78 municipalities in alphabetical order. The page opens on Ceiba, the study's case, unless the link names another. The left card holds the study's Table 11 variables and the Data Observatory's tourism supply. The right card has six groups of housing indicators. Each row has the label (press it for the full data), the rank among the 78 ('#n of 78'), the value with its margin, a small trend line with its length and, when the year differs, the year. A caution appears for municipalities with fewer than 25,000 residents. A link opens the municipality in the Data Observatory. The codes below list the rows of each card.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: housing.js (selectMuni, row, spark). The tourism and land-use rows read municipalities.json.
how_to_read: Use the rank and the trend line to place a municipality, and the margin to judge a small difference.
caveats: Ranks count only municipalities with a value. Tied values share the first of their places.
The affordability line says 'out of reach' when the rounded ratio is above 1. It uses the study's fixed 5% loan rate in every year.
Housing assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) counts approvals of owners and renters, not damaged homes.

In Snapshot 2026-10, 14 municipalities have no stop counted inside the border (for example Isabela, Yauco and Maricao). For them the card shows 0.0% of places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable and of any mapped stop, or 0.4% and 0.8% for Toa Alta and Arroyo. That means no stop was counted inside the municipality, not that no place is near transit. The 2D map leaves the share near any mapped stop blank for them.
The table numbers are those used on this page and in this dictionary. The study PDF numbers some tables differently (the Ceiba table is Table 13 in the PDF and Table 11 here).

name: Housing page: data catalog and search
plain: The Data section lists every dataset on the Housing page. Type in the box to find one, and press a name to open its full data.
definition: The catalog lists 58 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10: 46 survey, census, estimate and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) series, 3 land-use shares and 9 published or island-wide tables. Groups are Population, Housing stock, Households, Prices and incomes, Cost burden, Affordability, Disaster recovery and Land use, and then 'Published tables and island-wide series'. Each row gives the name, the source reference, the years it covers and a note when margins of error are published. The box 'Find a dataset' looks in the name, the reference and the group, ignoring accents and capitals, and the count beside it shows how many datasets match.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: housing.js (renderCatalog).
how_to_read: Use the group names to browse. Use the box when you know a word such as rent or vacancy.
caveats: The catalog counts datasets of this page. The Analysis tab lists more datasets and groups them differently.

name: Housing page: published tables beside live versions
plain: The Housing page shows Tables 2, 6, 7 and 10 of the 2023 study as printed, and for Tables 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7 a live version for the chosen year beside them. The table numbers are those used on this page and in this dictionary. The study PDF numbers some tables differently (for example the affordability table is Table 8 in the PDF and Table 6 here).
definition: The page shows Tables 2, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 of the 2023 study as printed, with the table numbers used on this page. For Tables 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7 it adds a live version for the chosen year, built from the American Community Survey (ACS) or from the Census Bureau's population estimates. Each table has a button to open the full table in the 'Full data' window. Printed and live versions use different years and methods. These ids work in the link ?d= (see the codes below).

coverage.frequency: Printed tables are fixed (2023). Live parts follow the year bar.

method: housing.js (renderTable2, renderTable6, renderTable7, renderBurdenCharts, renderPaperTables).
how_to_read: Read a printed table and its live version together. They use different years and methods.
caveats: The study's change columns compare 2012 with 2021 in nominal dollars. The live columns compare the base year with the chosen year, also nominal. The two can differ in sign. They are different measurements, not corrections of each other.
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) projects are shown as printed in the 2023 study. The table is not updated from the database of the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).
Locations on the LIHTC map are at the municipality, not at the project.

The cost and Community Development Block Grant for Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) amounts in Table 10 are estimates printed in the 2023 study and are not updated. They are the study's estimates, not a record of spending.
