values.population: Table 2, Puerto Rico's population change. Two menus 'Compare ... with ...' pick any two population years, and a line of the table uses them. The page also shows the study's printed figures and the census counts of 2010 and 2020.
values.table6: Table 6 as printed: maximum home loan by age of householder, 2021. The page repeats the same arithmetic for the chosen year's incomes.
values.t6live: Table 6 method for every ACS window: median income by age of householder and the maximum 30-year mortgage.
values.table7: Table 7: owner-occupied units by age of householder, as printed and for every ACS window. A chart shows the printed shares beside the chosen year.
values.table10: Table 10: LIHTC projects funded with CDBG-DR, as printed. A map shows one circle for each municipality, sized by units. The cost and CDBG-DR amounts are estimates printed in the 2023 study and are not updated.
values.grapilive: Table 3, live: gross rent as a share of income, every ACS window, island-wide (ACS table B25070). A chart shows the distribution for the chosen year, with the share paying 30% or more in red. The study's figure (52% of renters) is beside it.
values.smocapilive: Table 4, live: owner costs as a share of income with a mortgage, every ACS window, island-wide (ACS table B25091). A chart shows the distribution for the chosen year, with the share paying 30% or more in red. The study's figure (38% of owners with a mortgage) is beside it.

name: Housing page: income against home value (affordability chart)
plain: A chart plots each municipality's median household income against its median home value. A line marks where the typical home exactly equals the largest loan a household with that income can carry.
definition: Each dot is a municipality, for the survey window of the chosen year (the title says which). A red dot sits above the line: its median home value is higher than the maximum affordable loan for its median income. A green dot sits below the line. The line is drawn from zero income to 5% above the highest income. It uses the study's arithmetic: 30% of income for housing, 78% of that to principal and interest, a 30-year loan at a fixed 5%. A click on a dot selects the municipality. The chart's legend names the three marks.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

method: housing.js (renderScatter, payment).
how_to_read: Dots far above the line are municipalities where typical homes cost much more than typical incomes can borrow for.
caveats: The loan rate is fixed at 5% in every year. The Housing page notes that actual mortgage rates ranged from under 4% to over 7% over this period.
Median values and median incomes come from a survey with margins of error that are large in small municipalities.
The line is a screening test. It is not a lending rule and it ignores down payments, taxes and insurance.

view.label: Housing page: Home ownership affordability

name: Housing page: 'Latest data' and 'As published' numbers
plain: The top of the Housing page has two rows of large numbers. 'Latest data' has eight live Puerto Rico figures that open their full data. 'As published in the 2023 study' has six printed figures.
definition: Latest data holds eight figures. They are residents (population), the change since the 2020 census, housing units and the share of homes vacant. They also include 'other vacant' homes (the abandoned-housing proxy), the median home value, the share of renters who pay 30% or more of income on rent, and the affordability ratio (above 1 means out of reach). Each shows its source and year and opens its full data. As published holds five figures: housing units in 2020 (1.6 million), vacant homes in 2020 and the estimate of dilapidated or abandoned units. The others are the new homes needed each year (a government estimate) and the residents of the 2020 census (3,285,694).

coverage.frequency: Live figures follow the latest build. Printed figures are fixed.

method: housing.js (renderLatestKpis, renderPaperTables). The printed numbers are in housing.json.
how_to_read: Compare a live figure with its printed partner only when they describe the same thing and year.
caveats: Printed estimates (abandoned units, new homes needed) are the study's own estimates. They are not recalculated.
The printed 2020 residents figure (3,285,694) is 180 lower than the 2020 census count in the live series (3,285,874). The page shows both figures as their sources give them.

The printed 370,000 vacant homes is labelled Census 2020 on the page, but the 2020 census-day count of vacant units in the observatory's data is 257,625. The printed figure is close to survey estimates (368,182 for the 2015-2019 window). Treat it as the study's figure.

view.label: Housing page: headline numbers

name: Topics tab (the headline figure of each field)
plain: The Topics tab is what the 2D map shows first. It has one card for each field of the observatory, with a headline figure for the whole island, a small trend line when the figure has a history, and a button that puts its data on the map. Only the municipal boundaries are on the map at the start.
definition: The cards come from the domain registry through catalog.json, so a new field appears with no change to the page. A card has the field's name and description in the page language, a status ('Some data' or 'No data yet') when the field is not fully covered, and one block for the field's headline figure and one for each sub-field that has its own. A block has the name of the figure, its value, the period it covers ('Puerto Rico · 2020–2024, five-year estimate') and, for a yearly series, a trend line of the Puerto Rico value for every year. 'Show on map' puts the figure's data on the map: a yearly series is added to the Analysis tab, and a measure held for each municipality joins it too, as a dataset; both are listed in the On the map panel. 'What it means' opens the dictionary entry of the figure. 'Browse N documented items' opens the Catalog tab for the field. A field with no data yet says so. A field with datasets on the wish list gives their number and a button 'What is planned', which lists them: title, status (candidate, checked, building or blocked) and source, read from wanted.json when the button is pressed (about 21 KB compressed). The titles are in English for now. The tab ends with buttons for the Catalog tab and the chat, and a note on what the figures are.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot (python catalog.py, run by build.py after the dictionary). The nightly transit refresh does not rewrite it.

method: catalog.js (renderOverview, cardHtml, metricHtml, spark, apply) reads S.catalog, which app.js fetches at the start from data/catalog.json (the index of the dictionary is in catalog_index.json, which loads when the Catalog tab first opens), and data/wanted.json for the planned datasets. How each figure is worked out: methods.headline_figures.
how_to_read: Read each figure as the number for the whole of Puerto Rico over the period shown. It is not a score, and the fields are not ranked against one another. Press 'What it means' before you quote a figure: tourism figures count listings, and an estimate has a margin of error.
caveats: The names of the figures are in Spanish and English; the long text of the dictionary entries behind 'What it means' is English for now.
The trend line shows the Puerto Rico value for each year the series has. It starts at the lowest value of its own range, so two lines should not be compared by height.
'Show on map' for a yearly series opens the Analysis tab, which loads its data the first time (about 0.4 MB compressed).

view.label: 2D map, Topics tab

name: Catalog tab (find data and add it to the map)
plain: The Catalog tab searches everything the dictionary documents and puts it on the map with one button. You can filter by field, geography, year covered, license of the sources and source.
definition: The tab lists the dictionary's entries, 40 at a time. At first it lists only what can go on the map: a yearly series (it joins the Analysis tab), a measure held for each municipality (it shades the municipalities) or a layer (it is switched on). Clear 'Only what can go on the map' to list every entry, methods and categories included. The search box matches the name, the identifier and the field of an entry; on a Spanish page it also matches the Spanish name, where the entry has one, and the words of the entry's Spanish summary. The filters are Domain (the fields and sub-fields of the registry), Geography (the level of the published file an entry describes), Covers year, License of the sources (strictest) and Source. Each row shows the name, the field, the years, the geography and the license class, an 'Add to map' button when the entry can go on the map, and a link to its dictionary entry. 'Open these in the data dictionary' opens the dictionary with the same search and field.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot (python catalog.py, run by build.py after the dictionary). The nightly transit refresh does not rewrite it.

method: catalog.js (rows, results, rowHtml, apply) reads the index of the dictionary in catalog_index.json, which it fetches the first time the tab opens, with the Spanish names of the entries (site/i18n/es.map.catalog.js) and, on a Spanish page, the words of the Spanish summaries (catalog_es.json). How an entry goes on the map is worked out when the catalog is built (catalog.py map_action): from where the entry says its data live (a yearly series, a field of municipalities.json) or, for a layer, from the list in dictionary_src/map_layers.json. It is checked again in the page: the button appears only when the page knows the target and the menu offers it.
how_to_read: Use it to find a dataset by topic, then open its dictionary entry before you rely on it. The geography, the years and the license class are there to help you choose, not to replace the entry.
caveats: In Spanish most names of the data stay in English for now; the search also finds an entry by the words of its Spanish summary.

The license is the strictest class among the entry's sources, as recorded in the sources list. It is not a legal review, and it can be strict for an entry that only cites a study. Open the entry to see which source sets it.
An entry with no file or layer link has no 'Add to map' button, although it may be documented.
Adding a layer to the map does not remove the layers already on it. Switch layers off in the Map layers tab or the Analysis tab.

view.label: 2D map, Catalog tab

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser from the datasets of the Analysis tab, each time the view is drawn

name: Workbench: Correlations tab (correlation matrix)
plain: A table of the correlation between every pair of visible layers, so you can see at a glance which ones move together across the municipalities.
definition: Up to eight visible layers, each as it is on the map (its year, rescaling and settings). Each cell gives r and n, the number of municipalities that have a value for both layers of the pair; each pair uses its own municipalities (pairwise complete), so n can differ between cells. Pearson measures a straight-line pattern; Spearman (rank order) measures whether the ranks rise or fall together, which a few very large values do not dominate. A pair with fewer than 3 municipalities gets no r. Colours: dark red below −0.5, light red −0.5 to −0.1, grey −0.1 to 0.1, light blue 0.1 to 0.5, dark blue above 0.5.
method: economy.js (ecBenchMatrix) with Core.stats.matrix and Core.stats.correlation (site/js/core/stats.js; Spearman is Pearson on the ranks, ties sharing the mean of their ranks).
how_to_read: Read a cell as a pattern across places: a dark blue cell means municipalities with more of one tend to have more of the other. Check n before comparing two cells.
caveats: A correlation across places is not cause and effect, and it does not describe the people inside a place.
Large places, survey noise and a third factor can drive a correlation.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab (press Workbench, then Correlations)

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser from the datasets of the Analysis tab, each time the view is drawn

name: Workbench: Small multiples tab
plain: Many small maps side by side: one map for each year of a layer, or one map for each visible layer, so changes and differences show at a glance.
definition: 'One map for each year of one layer' draws the chosen layer in each of its last 12 years that have values, with one set of classes for every map (worked out from all the years together), so a colour means the same in each year; the Puerto Rico value is under each map. 'One map for each visible layer' draws up to eight visible layers at the year each shows, each with its own classes, so colours are not comparable between maps. Hover a municipality for its value. The maps have no base map.
method: economy.js (ecBenchMultiples, ecClassFill) with Core.minimap (site/js/core/minimap.js), which draws the 78 municipal outlines as SVG.
how_to_read: In the maps by year, a municipality that darkens from map to map is rising against the same classes.
caveats: In the maps by layer each map has its own classes: compare where values are high or low, not the colours.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser from the datasets of the Analysis tab, each time the view is drawn

name: Workbench: Compare two maps tab (swipe)
plain: Two layers on one map of Puerto Rico with a divider you can drag: the left side shows one layer and the right side the other.
definition: Pick the left and the right layer among the visible layers. The slider moves the divider across the island; each side keeps its own classes and has its own legend below the map. Hovering a municipality gives both values. The slider works with the keyboard (arrow keys).
method: economy.js (ecBenchSwipe): one SVG with the second layer clipped at the divider.
how_to_read: Move the divider slowly over a region to see whether the two layers are high in the same places.
caveats: The two sides have different classes: a dark colour on each side means high for that layer, not the same number.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab (press Workbench, then Compare two maps)

name: Area profile page (profile.html)
plain: One page for each municipio with every dataset of the observatory for that place, grouped by field, with its rank among the 78 municipios, Puerto Rico's value and its trend.
definition: Open it from a municipality on the map (the pop-up's 'Area profile' link or the Municipality tab) or as profile.html?area= and the municipio's five-digit code (72127 is San Juan). The page reads the same files as the Analysis tab. Each field of the registry has a table; each row is a dataset with its latest value as published and its margin of error, the value a shaded map compares (per 1,000 residents, per resident or a share), its rank among the municipios that have a value (1 is the highest), Puerto Rico's value on the same measure, and a trend line of up to 15 years. Datasets with no value for the place are left out, unless an empty place has a meaning (a shortage area: 'No area shortage designation'). A small map marks the municipio and its five similar municipios. 'Download CSV' saves the rows.

coverage.frequency: Built in your browser from the published files of the snapshot

method: profile.js with Core.datasets (the list of files the Analysis tab also reads), Core.engine, Core.stats and Core.minimap. The page draws its first field (Housing) and the similar municipios as soon as their files arrive, then fetches the other files and draws every field; until then it says it is loading the other fields, and 'Download CSV' waits for them.
how_to_read: A rank says where the place stands among the municipios, not whether that is good: rank 1 in poverty is the highest poverty.
caveats: Datasets of different years sit side by side: read each row's year.
Survey values have margins of error; read them before comparing two places.

name: Workbench: Scenarios tab (save, compare, model outputs)
plain: Save what the map shows as a scenario, compare two scenarios figure by figure, and load the results of an outside model as a layer marked as model output, not observed data.
definition: A scenario keeps the map's link (layers, year, composite, planned route), the figures it produced (the planned route's measures and Puerto Rico's value of each visible layer, with its year and settings) and any model output loaded with it. Scenarios stay in the browser (IndexedDB); 'Export' saves one as a JSON file and 'Import a scenario' reads it back after checking it. 'Open scenario' restores the view, and its model outputs, from the link. 'Compare two scenarios' lists every figure with A, B, B − A and the change in percent; when both scenarios hold a model output of the same variable, 'Map B − A' shades the difference. Names, labels and notes refuse e-mail addresses and telephone numbers: a scenario names a team or organisation, not a person's contact.

coverage.frequency: Kept in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere

method: js/scenarios.js (loaded the first time the tab opens) and Core.scenario (site/js/core/scenario.js: make, check, read, diff, parseModel, diffSeries); economy.js (ecBenchScenarios, ecScenarioLib). The link part sc= reopens a scenario that holds model outputs.
how_to_read: A difference between two scenarios is the difference between two views or two model runs, not a forecast.
caveats: Scenarios live in this browser only: clearing the browser's data deletes them. Export the ones to keep.
A figure saved with one year or setting is another figure from the same dataset with another year or setting.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab (press Workbench, then Scenarios)

name: Workbench: Study areas tab (your own polygons, summarised)
plain: Load your own polygons, such as a neighbourhood or a service area, and see what each holds: residents, transit stops and, on request, tourism places and flood and protected land, plus every dataset of the Analysis tab estimated for each area.
definition: A GeoJSON file of polygons in longitude and latitude, up to 200 areas, is read in the browser and never uploaded; only each area's name and shape are kept, with the set's name, source and description, in IndexedDB. For each area: its km², residents by Census 2020 block centroid, residents more than 800 m from a scheduled stop, scheduled transit stops and, on request, tourism places and the share of its land in a FEMA flood hazard area (zones A and V) and in a protected area. Every dataset of the Analysis tab is estimated for each area from the municipios it covers: totals by the share of each municipio's residents inside (land, for totals measured in km²), an exact sum when the area holds whole municipios; rates and levels as an average weighted by the residents inside. Each row names its method.
geography: Polygons the user loads, within Puerto Rico

coverage.frequency: Kept in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere

method: js/studyareas.js (loaded the first time the tab opens) and Core.study (site/js/core/study.js: parse, make, check, read, toGeoJSON, measure, estimate); economy.js (ecBenchStudy, ecStudyLib). docs/study-areas.md.
how_to_read: The estimates assume a municipio is the same throughout: a small area inside one municipio gets that municipio's rate. Counted measures (residents, stops, places) are counts inside the area; the dataset rows are estimates.
caveats: Study areas live in this browser only: clearing the browser's data deletes them. Export the ones to keep.
Survey margins of error are not carried into the estimates.
Residents are placed at the centre of their census block, so a block cut by an edge counts wholly on the side of its centre.

name: Land-use analysis (2D map)
plain: A panel that shows how the land of Puerto Rico and of each municipality divides among the classes of the 2015 land use plan, as bars and tables, with all 78 municipalities side by side. It opens from the Land use group of the Map layers tab.
definition: The button 'Land use by municipality and for Puerto Rico', in the Land use group of the Map layers tab, opens a panel under the map (it replaces the Economy workbench while open). It shows the chosen area (Puerto Rico or a municipality) as one bar split by class, with the km² and the share of land of each, and the 78 municipalities as bars sorted by the share of a class you choose. It can show the ten classes of the legend or the four groups (urban, for urban growth, ordinary rural, specially protected rural). Clicking a municipality shows it and moves the map there. The CSV holds the km² and shares of every area.
method: js/landuse_view.js reads landuse_summary.json and divides each class (or group) by the land of the area in the plan: the sum of the classes with in_share, so water and road rights-of-way are left out. Nothing is computed from the map's simplified polygons.
source_detail: landuse_summary.json (landuse.py class_summary); the script js/landuse_view.js loads the first time the panel opens.

coverage.frequency: A single plan version, dated 30 November 2015.

how_to_read: Each bar is 100% of the land in the plan of that area; water and road rights-of-way are left out. Hover a segment for its class and share. The table under the chosen area gives the exact figures.
caveats: A planning classification, not land cover.
The analysis always shows every class: unticking a class in the legend hides it on the map only.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab, Land use: Land use by municipality and for Puerto Rico

name: Shading the Analysis tab's map by barrio
plain: A shaded layer of the Analysis tab can be drawn on the 901 barrios instead of the 78 municipalities, for the datasets that have values for barrios: the American Community Survey estimates (population, housing, income, age and the others of acs_barrio.json). Datasets published only by municipality, such as jobs and wages, have no barrio values and keep the municipal map.
definition: In the Analysis tab, Settings of a shaded layer, Area: Municipalities or Barrios. The choice is offered when the dataset is in acs_barrio.json (the data dictionary lists the barrio level for it) and the layer is the only shaded one; symbols and two shaded layers together stay municipal. The barrio values are the American Community Survey 5-year estimates for the 901 Census county subdivisions, with their margins of error: a barrio whose margin is above 30% of its estimate is hatched, as on the municipal map. A value is shown as published or as a percentile among the barrios; the rescalings that need a municipio's residents or land (per 1,000 residents, per km², share of Puerto Rico) fall back to the published value, and the legend says so. Hovering a barrio shows its name, municipality, value and margin of error. The link keeps the choice (mode code b). The workbench views, the table and the click pop-ups stay municipal.

coverage.frequency: The survey windows of acs_barrio.json.

method: js/econ_level.js, loaded the first time a layer asks for it, reads the engine's contract for the layer at the barrio level (E.series with level 'barrio', from acs_barrio.json via economy.js ecLoadLevel), cuts five classes from the barrio values with the layer's own method (quantiles, equal intervals, natural breaks or own limits) and colours barrios.geojson by them.
source_detail: acs_barrio.json (American Community Survey 5-year estimates for county subdivisions); barrios.geojson (Census TIGERweb county subdivisions).
how_to_read: Small areas have wide margins: in the 2020-2024 window, 387 of the 901 barrios have a less reliable median household income and 112 have none. Read the hatching before comparing two barrios, and use the CSV by area for the exact margins.
caveats: Only datasets with barrio values in the files: municipal-only datasets are not split among barrios, because no source gives their barrio values and the observatory does not estimate them.
Barrios are Census county subdivisions; their boundaries are those of 2020.
